Check the tree and proposed work before excavation

Gate posts, foundations, tracks, drainage and cable routes can affect nearby trees as well as the entrance. Start by identifying the trees and discussing the proposed work with the local planning authority and a competent arboricultural adviser where needed.

Check Tree Preservation Orders, conservation-area status and relevant conditions on existing planning permissions. Do not assume permission for a gate authorises all work affecting a tree.

What a Tree Preservation Order can restrict

A Tree Preservation Order protects specified trees, groups or woodlands. Government guidance identifies prohibited activities without the authority’s written consent, including cutting down, topping, lopping, uprooting, wilful damage and destruction. It also explains that cutting roots can require consent.

The work, exemptions and procedure need checking for the actual circumstances. Consult GOV.UK guidance on protected trees and the relevant local authority before carrying out work.

Conservation-area trees need a separate check

A tree can be subject to conservation-area controls even where it is not covered by a Tree Preservation Order. Notification requirements and exceptions depend on the circumstances. Ask the council which process applies and allow for it before agreeing a start date.

A borough label or generic website statement cannot confirm the status of your tree. Keep the authority’s response, any consent and its conditions with the project records.

Give the adviser the full entrance layout

Show the proposed gate, supports, motor or track, power cable, drainage and paving changes. Include temporary construction access, storage and vehicle movements. An excavation outside the visible canopy is not automatically clear of roots.

Ask the arboricultural adviser and gate contractor to coordinate the required protection area, access restrictions and construction method. Do not substitute a simple trunk-distance formula or a permitted percentage of root loss for that assessment.

Agree the method and responsibilities in writing

The proposal should identify who will obtain information or consent, which work is permitted, the protection arrangements and any supervision required. Where the layout needs to change to avoid harm, update the gate drawings and quotation before construction.

This article does not prescribe air-spading pressures, root barriers or a universal foundation detail. Those choices need site-specific advice. Do not cut exposed roots or alter the agreed method to keep a gate job moving; stop the affected work and obtain advice.

Prepare the enquiry and compare the scope

Send the property location, photographs from accessible positions and a description of the entrance work you want. Share tree reports, council responses and existing plans if you have them. Ask which specialist work falls within the gate quotation and which needs a separate appointment.

Our gate quotation checklist helps identify exclusions. Discuss the gate project before commissioning equipment that may not fit the agreed protected-tree layout.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a gate project need checks for nearby tree roots?+
Yes. Foundations, tracks, cables, drainage and construction access can affect roots. Check protected status and obtain competent advice for the proposed work before excavation.
Does gate planning permission automatically allow root cutting?+
Do not assume that it does. Ask the local authority which permissions, tree consents, conditions or notifications apply to the actual work.
Can I use a standard distance from the trunk for the gate post?+
A generic distance is not a site design. Ask the relevant adviser and contractor to establish the protection and construction arrangements for the tree and entrance.

What underground gate automation means

An underground swing-gate operator places much of the drive assembly in a foundation box near the hinge. This can reduce the equipment visible on the leaf, which may suit an entrance where appearance matters. Covers, release arrangements and other controls can remain visible.

The operator is one part of the entrance. The installer still needs to assess the gate, hinges, supports, exposure and movement. Concealing a motor does not make an unsuitable gate ready for automation.

Drainage and access belong in the design

Ask how the foundation box will drain at your property and who provides that work. Tell the installer about standing water and previous flooding. Discuss how the covers will remain accessible after paving, planting or resurfacing.

The quotation should identify excavation, foundations, cable routes, drainage and reinstatement. Ask how future maintenance or replacement can take place without unnecessary damage to the finished driveway.

Compare visible operators too

An above-ground arm may involve a different set of alterations and maintenance access. Compare both options against the hinge geometry, required opening angle and appearance of the whole entrance.

Request the proposed model and its suitability assessment. Voltage alone does not tell you whether a motor uses a hydraulic mechanism or what upkeep it needs. Follow the instructions for the specified equipment.

Keep release and handover practical

Ask for a demonstration of the actual manual release and how the leaf is controlled and secured afterwards. Keep the correct key and instructions accessible. Do not assume that every underground release sits in the same place.

Explore electric swing gates and our retrofit quotation guide. For an existing fault, arrange repair assessment before opening a motor enclosure.

Provide photographs of the full entrance, the hinge areas and the finished ground from safe positions. Explain whether the gate is existing or new, whether the driveway will be resurfaced and where water collects after rain. Ask the installer to identify any further structural or drainage investigation needed before quoting.

Have the proposed drawing show the relationship between the gate pivot and the operator, together with foundation boxes, covers and cable routes. Request confirmation of the opening angle and the space the leaf occupies throughout travel. Do not assume that a concealed operator removes restrictions caused by a rising driveway.

For a retrofit, ask whether the existing hinges, posts and gate construction can work with the proposed operator. Identify any lifting, alterations or temporary removal in the quotation. Include safe access arrangements for residents while the entrance is unavailable.

Compare the camera and conversation at your gate

If an existing intercom rings but fails to open the gate, describe that symptom before buying a replacement panel.   • Terms: VAT, equipment warranty, workmanship cover, exclusions and charges for a return visit.

Accounts, updates and support after installation

Agree who owns the administrator account, controls recovery details and can remove a user. Keep the equipment list, written terms and handover records together. Discuss video intercom installation with that brief so the quotation addresses your entrance and the people who use it.

Agree preparation and repair methods

The proposed method should suit the metal, condition and existing coatings. Ask how the contractor will assess unknown old paint and manage dust, waste and nearby surfaces. Do not start abrasive stripping or heating from a generic restoration recipe.

If the boundary is listed or has conservation controls, check required advice or consent before removing fabric. Read our conservation-area guide and record any conditions in the scope.

Choose a finish for the exterior gate

Compare physical samples for colour, sheen and texture. Ask how the coating system treats joints, edges, repaired areas and the back face. Confirm which preparation and coating stages form part of the quotation.

For a period entrance, compare the gate with the railings, piers and house details. There is no universal heritage-grade finish that replaces an assessment of the actual material and conservation context. Request care instructions and written finish terms.

Assess automation separately

A restored appearance does not establish suitability for powered movement. Ask for assessment of the hinges, supports, geometry, exposure and hazards around the opening before adding a drive.

Compare repair and replacement proposals with equivalent finishing and handover scope. Discuss metal gate options or gate repairs using photographs and your existing service records.

Ask for an assessment-to-handover programme

Start with photographs and an inventory of the gate, matching railings, hinges and decorative pieces. Ask the specialist to separate urgent stability concerns, repairable damage and finish deterioration. Agree whether further findings may emerge after appropriate preparation exposes the material.

The written programme should explain temporary access, removal if needed, transport, workshop or on-site work, finish stages and refitting. Identify who deals with posts, masonry and automation where those fall outside the metalworker’s scope. Record how additional repairs will be priced and authorised.

At completion, compare the work with the inventory and agreed drawings. Ask for the repair record, finish specification and care instructions. For a powered entrance, arrange the relevant gate-system checks after refitting rather than assuming workshop restoration completes the whole job.

Car Park Barriers and Access Control in London

A barrier is the simplest way to stop your car park filling with people who shouldn’t be there. Commuters use office spaces, shoppers take residents’ bays, and vans get dumped overnight. We design, supply and install car park barriers, vehicle detection and access control for offices, apartment blocks, retail sites, hospitals, schools and private car parks across London. That covers single-lane entrances, full entry and exit layouts, and underground car parks.

Types of barrier

A standard boom barrier has a single straight arm, typically 3 to 6 metres long, and suits most surface car parks. It’s the cheapest and simplest option, and a good barrier opens in around three to six seconds.

High-speed barriers open in a second or two. They’re for busy entrances where a queue would otherwise back up onto the road, such as staff car parks at shift change and retail sites at peak times.

Folding-arm barriers have a hinged arm that folds as it rises, so it fits under a low ceiling. They’re the usual answer for underground and multi-storey car parks with limited headroom, often paired with a height-restriction bar at the entrance so oversized vans don’t hit the structure.

Skirted barriers have a hanging mesh or rail skirt below the arm, which stops pedestrians, cyclists and mopeds slipping underneath. They’re useful where the barrier is the only control on the entrance.

For higher-security sites, rising bollards or road blockers stop a vehicle physically rather than just signalling it to stop. They cost considerably more.

How vehicles are detected

Most barriers rely on induction loops: wire loops cut into the road surface that sense the metal of a car above them. A safety loop under the arm stops it coming down onto a vehicle. An exit loop can lift the barrier automatically for cars leaving the site, so nobody needs a fob to get out. A closing loop lowers the arm as soon as each car has passed, which cuts down tailgating. Photocells add a second layer of protection, especially for higher vehicles and pedestrians.

How drivers get in

ANPR (automatic number plate recognition) reads the number plate and lifts the barrier for registered vehicles. There’s nothing to hand out, and visitors can be pre-registered through an online portal by reception or residents. It needs a well-positioned camera and good lighting, and it struggles with dirty or non-standard plates. Most sites keep a back-up method alongside it. See ANPR systems.

Long-range tags stick to the windscreen and are read from several metres away. They’re very reliable and fast, so they suit staff and residents who arrive every day.

Proximity fobs and cards are read by a post-mounted reader at window height. They’re cheap and easy to manage, but the driver has to stop and reach out.

Intercoms let visitors and delivery drivers call reception, a concierge or a remote monitoring service, who then lifts the barrier. A video intercom lets staff see who they’re letting in. GSM phone entry lets authorised users open the barrier by calling it from their mobile.

On pay-to-park sites, ticketing and payment are handled by specialist parking management systems. We install and maintain the barriers and detection and work alongside the payment provider you choose.

Layout and queuing

The barrier should sit far enough back from the road that a car waiting at it, plus any car behind, is fully off the highway. On busy sites that may mean space for two or three cars. Reader posts and intercoms are set at driver’s-window height and positioned so the driver can reach them without leaving the car. Entry and exit lanes with a central island are easier to manage than a single shared lane. People on foot should have their own route beside the barrier, not one that crosses in front of a moving arm.

ANPR and your data

Number plates are personal data, so an ANPR system brings legal duties under UK GDPR. You’ll need signs telling drivers that ANPR is in use, a clear policy on how long plate data is kept, and someone responsible for who can see it. We set the system up with sensible retention settings and can advise on signage. The legal responsibility sits with the site operator.

Barrier or gate?

A barrier controls vehicles but doesn’t secure a site. Anyone on foot can walk round it, and a determined driver can drive through it. Many sites use a barrier for the working day and a sliding or swing gate to lock the car park at night. If you need to keep people out as well as cars, see industrial security gates or heavy-duty sliding gates.

Installation

A barrier is bolted to a concrete base, with ducting for power and control cables. Induction loops are cut into the road surface and sealed. Most single-lane installations take one day on site, with the entrance closed for part of it. We plan the work for quiet periods, evenings or weekends where the car park can’t close during the day. At handover, the site team is shown how to manage users, release the barrier by hand, and what to do if the arm is hit.

Powered barriers come under the same safety standards and HSE guidance as powered gates. That means safety loops and photocells, recorded safety tests, and regular servicing.

Cost of car park barriers in London

As a rough guide, a standard barrier with induction loops and a fob reader typically costs £3,000 to £6,000 installed, per lane. High-speed and folding-arm barriers usually cost £5,000 to £9,000. Adding ANPR is typically £2,500 to £6,000 per lane, plus an ongoing software or support subscription on most systems. Look at the running costs too: replacement fobs or tags, SIM connectivity for intercoms and GSM units, software licences and service contracts. Every quote sets these out separately, so you can compare like with like.

Servicing and damage

Barriers on busy car parks cycle hundreds of times a day and should be serviced two to four times a year. Arms do get hit. A good barrier has a breakaway arm fixing that protects the motor when that happens, and keeping a spare arm on site means the entrance is back in use the same day. For a barrier that’s already faulty, see gate repair and servicing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a barrier give the same security as a gate?+
No. A barrier controls vehicles, but people on foot can walk round it. Use a gate, or a barrier plus a gate locked out of hours, if you need to secure the site itself.
Can you add number plate recognition to an existing barrier?+
Usually, yes. We check the barrier’s controller, the camera position and the power and network connections at survey. Older barriers sometimes need a new controller to work reliably with ANPR.
What happens if the power fails?+
The barrier can be lifted by hand with a release key. Battery backup or a setting that raises the arm on power loss is worth considering for sites where vehicles must always be able to leave.
What should a barrier quotation include?+
The barrier model, groundworks, loops, access control equipment, commissioning, training and making good, with VAT, exclusions and any ongoing subscriptions or service charges shown separately. Ours do.
Can the barrier work with an underground car park’s low ceiling?+
Yes. A folding-arm barrier rises within a much lower height than a straight arm. We measure the clear headroom at survey.

Heavy-Duty Commercial Sliding Gates in London

Sliding gates are the workhorse of commercial entrances. They handle wide openings, they don’t swing into traffic or across a pavement, and a well-built one will run thousands of times a month for years. We design, supply and install heavy-duty sliding gates for warehouses, depots, yards, car parks, apartment blocks and business premises across London. That covers new installations, motor upgrades and repairs to existing commercial gates.

Cantilever, tracked, telescopic or bi-parting

The first decision is how the gate is supported, and that’s mostly decided by how much space you have beside the opening.

Cantilever gates hang from two roller carriages fixed to a concrete foundation beside the opening. Nothing touches the ground across the entrance itself. Lorries cross a clean threshold, and grit, ice and debris can’t stop the gate. To balance, the gate needs a tail behind the opening, usually around 40 to 50 percent of the opening’s width. An 8-metre opening therefore needs roughly 12 metres of straight, level fence line for the gate to slide back along. Cantilever is the first choice for most commercial sites where that space exists.

Tracked gates run on wheels along a steel rail set into or bolted onto the ground. They only need side space roughly equal to the opening, so they fit where a cantilever won’t. The catch is the track itself. It has to be kept clear and needs drainage, and on sites with heavy plant, loose aggregate or frequent ice it becomes the weak point.

Telescopic gates split into two or more leaves that slide over each other. That roughly halves the side space needed, which helps on tight London plots where the boundary turns a corner or meets a building close to the entrance.

Bi-parting gates use two sliding leaves meeting in the middle. They suit very wide openings, or sites with space on both sides of the entrance but not enough on either side for a single gate.

Motors, speed and duty

A commercial sliding gate typically weighs anywhere from 500 kg to over two tonnes, depending on width, height and infill. The motor is chosen by two numbers. One is the maximum gate weight it can drive. The other is its duty rating, meaning how many cycles an hour it can run without overheating. A motor sized for a domestic drive on a busy commercial entrance burns out, often within months.

For busy sites we use three-phase motors with inverter (variable-speed) drives. These start and stop the gate gently, which takes the shock out of the rack, rollers and frame, and they can run the gate faster through the middle of its travel. Lighter-use sites can run on single-phase power. If your site doesn’t have a three-phase supply near the entrance, the survey flags it early, because it affects both cost and programme.

The drive rack should be galvanised steel on any commercial gate. Nylon racks are fine on light domestic gates but wear quickly under heavy loads.

Infill and wind

Open infill such as 358 anti-climb mesh, steel palisade or vertical bars keeps the gate light and lets wind pass through. Solid cladding gives privacy and hides the yard, but it turns the gate into a sail. A solid 10-metre gate in an exposed position puts large sideways loads on its posts and rollers, so it needs a heavier structure and motor. If you want screening, perforated or louvred panels are often a better compromise than fully solid sheeting.

Safety

Sliding gates are dangerous in two places: the closing edge, where the gate meets the catch post, and the points where it slides past fixed posts and rollers, where hands and arms can be drawn in. Every gate we install has safety edges on the leading and trailing edges and photocells on both sides of the opening. Mesh is covered with fine guarding where the gate passes the posts. Closing forces are tested and recorded against BS EN 12453. A powered commercial gate must also meet the product standard BS EN 13241 and be supplied with the matching UKCA or CE marking and declaration. Ask for those documents from any installer.

The HSE’s guidance on powered gates makes clear that whoever controls the site is responsible for keeping a powered gate safe. Regular servicing with written records is how you show you’ve done that.

Groundworks and installation

A cantilever gate stands on a reinforced concrete foundation beam that carries the whole weight of the gate on two points. Getting it level and the right size matters more than anything else on the job. We also lay ducting for power and control cables, plus drainage for tracked gates. London sites often have shallow services, so we scan for buried cables and pipes before digging.

Installation usually takes two visits. The first covers groundworks and foundations. The second, about a week later once the concrete has cured, is for hanging the gate, fitting the motor and commissioning. On sites that have to stay operational, the old gate or temporary fencing stays in place until the new gate is working.

Upgrading an existing sliding gate

Plenty of commercial sliding gates have a sound frame but a tired or underpowered motor, worn rollers, or no modern safety devices. In those cases, a new motor, new carriages and safety edges can give the gate years more life for a fraction of the cost of a replacement. Where the structure itself is failing, or a tracked gate keeps jamming, we’ll tell you so. A replacement cantilever gate is often cheaper over five years than repairing an unsuitable gate again and again. For faults on a gate you already have, see gate repair and servicing.

Access control

Sliding gates work with every type of access control: ANPR for fleet and staff vehicles, fobs and cards, video intercoms for visitors (with a second cab-height panel for lorry drivers), and GSM phone entry for opening from a mobile. For broader planning of security, traffic and pedestrian routes on an industrial site, see industrial security gates.

Cost of heavy-duty commercial sliding gates in London

As a rough guide, a powered cantilever gate for a 6-metre opening typically costs £10,000 to £18,000 installed. Openings of 10 metres and over usually run from £18,000 to £35,000, depending on height, infill, groundworks and power supply. Tracked gates generally come in somewhat cheaper. Replacing the motor on a sound existing gate is usually £2,500 to £6,000. Every quote is itemised and fixed in writing after survey.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a cantilever gate suitable for any commercial entrance?+
No. It needs a clear, fairly level run beside the opening, usually about one and a half times the opening’s width. If you don’t have that, a tracked, telescopic or bi-parting gate is the alternative. The survey measures this precisely.
How many times a day can the gate run?+
That depends on the motor’s duty rating, not the gate. Tell us your busiest hour as well as your daily total, and we’ll specify a motor rated above that demand.
What happens in a power cut?+
The motor has a manual release, so the gate can be pushed open by hand. Battery backup can keep the gate running for a limited number of cycles, and is worth having on sites where vehicles must keep moving.
Can you upgrade our existing sliding gate?+
Often, yes. We assess the frame, foundation, rollers and motor and tell you what can be kept. Adding safety edges and photocells to an older gate is one of the most common upgrades we do.
How long does installation take?+
Usually two site visits about a week apart, so the foundations can cure. Wider gates or projects with new power supplies or extensive groundworks take longer, and the quote sets out the programme.

Industrial Security Gates in London

Industrial gates take more punishment than anything on a domestic drive. They open dozens or hundreds of times a day, they have lorries reversing near them, and they may be the only thing between your stock and a thief with an angle grinder. We design, supply and install sliding, speed and swing gates, palisade and mesh fencing, and access control for warehouses, depots, yards, builders’ merchants and industrial estates across London.

Choosing the right gate type

Cantilever sliding gates are the standard choice for industrial entrances. The gate hangs from rollers on posts beside the opening instead of running on a ground track, so grit, ice, pallets and debris can’t jam it. A single leaf can span a very wide opening, comfortably wide enough for an articulated lorry. The trade-off is space. The gate needs a straight run alongside the fence, longer than the opening itself, because part of the frame acts as a counterweight. Our heavy-duty sliding gates page covers these in more detail.

Tracked sliding gates run on a rail set in the ground. They need less run-back than a cantilever gate, but the track has to be kept clear. That makes them a weaker choice for yards with loose material or heavy plant crossing the threshold.

Speed gates are bi-folding gates driven by powerful motors. They open in a few seconds rather than the 20 to 30 seconds a typical sliding gate takes. They suit busy entrances where vehicles would otherwise queue onto the road, and sites where tailgating through a slow-closing gate is a security problem. They fold back within their own posts, so they need very little side space. They cost more than a sliding gate.

Swing gates are the cheapest powered option and work where there’s room for the leaves to open fully without clashing with waiting or turning vehicles. Wide leaves with solid infill catch the wind badly, so on exposed sites they need heavier hinges and operators, or a different gate type.

Barriers control vehicles but don’t secure a perimeter. Many sites use a barrier for the busy working day and a gate to lock the site at night. See car park barriers.

Security ratings

If your insurer, landlord or tender asks for a rated gate, you’ll normally see one of two standards. LPS 1175 (from the Loss Prevention Certification Board) rates how long a gate or fence resists a deliberate forced attack, and with what tools. Lower ratings cover hand tools; higher ones cover extended attack with powered cutting equipment. Hostile vehicle mitigation ratings (PAS 68, IWA 14 and ISO 22343) are crash-tested ratings for stopping a vehicle being driven through the entrance. They’re usually only needed for critical infrastructure and high-risk sites.

A rating applies to the exact tested product, including its posts, foundations and locking. A heavy-looking palisade gate isn’t rated just because it looks strong. If you need a rating, we’ll supply the certification for the specific gate and configuration in the quote.

Most sites don’t need a formal rating. For them, the practical choices are what count: anti-climb mesh (358 mesh is the common high-security standard) or triple-pointed steel palisade, a height of 2.4 to 3 metres, no horizontal rails on the outside to climb, and shrouded hinges and locks that can’t easily be cut.

Planning for lorries and busy periods

Tell us the largest vehicle that uses the entrance and how it arrives. A 16.5-metre articulated lorry needs room to swing in. It also needs somewhere to wait while the gate opens that isn’t across the pavement or the road. On many London sites, that means setting the gate back from the boundary so the longest vehicle can stand clear of the highway.

Peak traffic matters as much as total traffic. A depot where 20 vans return at the end of a shift needs a faster gate and smarter access control than a warehouse with the same number of movements spread across the day. Motors are selected for their duty rating, meaning how many cycles an hour they can run without overheating. That’s why a domestic gate motor fails quickly on an industrial site.

Keep people on foot separate from vehicles. A pedestrian gate or turnstile beside the vehicle entrance stops staff and visiting drivers walking through the path of a moving gate.

Access control for staff, fleet and visitors

ANPR cameras open the gate automatically for registered vehicles. They’re ideal for fleet and staff parking (see ANPR systems). Staff on foot use fobs or cards, which can be cancelled individually and can log who came in and when. Visiting drivers use an intercom to reception or the gatehouse. For lorries, the intercom needs a second, higher panel at cab height, so the driver doesn’t have to climb down onto a live entrance.

On multi-tenant industrial estates, an intercom with a directory lets visitors call the right unit. Each tenant manages their own staff fobs, and the estate manager controls the gate itself.

Installation on a working site

Most industrial sites can’t simply close for a week. We phase the work so one side of the entrance stays usable, put temporary fencing in overnight where the perimeter is opened up, and schedule groundworks and gate hanging around your deliveries and shift patterns. Before work starts, we agree a method statement covering traffic management, pedestrian routes and who on your side is the point of contact. Heavier gates and fast motors may need a new three-phase or upgraded power supply. We identify that at survey so it doesn’t hold up the programme.

At handover you get operating instructions, training for the people who’ll run the entrance, safety test records and a log of who controls access permissions.

Cost of industrial security gates in London

Speed gates usually cost £20,000 to £45,000. LPS 1175 rated gates cost significantly more than unrated equivalents. Every quote is itemised and fixed in writing after survey.

Servicing and breakdowns

High-use gates wear quickly and should be serviced every quarter, with safety devices and closing forces tested at each visit. Under HSE guidance on powered gates, the site operator is responsible for keeping them safe, and written service records are your evidence that you have. We offer service contracts with the visit frequency and breakdown response times set out in writing. For a gate that’s already faulty, see gate repair and servicing.

Yes. Tell us the rating your insurer or specification requires, and the quote will include the certification for the exact gate and configuration.

Not automatically. Breakdown response is part of a service contract, with the response times and charges set out in writing. Sites that can’t operate with the gate down usually choose a contract with a guaranteed response.

How a well-planned school entrance works

Most schools work best with vehicle and pedestrian routes kept separate. The vehicle gate stays shut during arrival and collection, when the pavement is busiest with children. Staff parking and deliveries are timed around those windows, or routed through a second entrance if the site has one.

Pedestrian gates are usually left open for the morning arrival period and then locked. From then on, visitors enter only through a controlled point: a gate with a video intercom to the school office, released remotely once the visitor has been identified. On larger sites, an airlock (a small fenced holding area between the outer gate and the building) stops a visitor reaching the playground or entrance until reception has let them through the second gate. Staff use a fob, card or code. Fobs and cards are easiest to manage, because a lost or leaver’s fob is cancelled without changing anyone else’s access.

Fire safety has to be planned in from the start. Any electrically locked gate on an escape route needs to release when the fire alarm sounds, or have a clearly marked manual release. That decision is made with the school’s fire risk assessment, not after the gate is installed. Vehicle gates also need a way for the fire brigade to get in out of hours, usually a key switch or a link to the alarm system.

Choosing the right gates

For vehicle entrances where children walk nearby, sliding gates are usually the better choice. They don’t swing out across the pavement or playground, and they handle wide openings well. Any powered gate on a school site needs photocells and safety edges, and closing forces must be tested against BS EN 12453. Mesh or bar infill needs guarding where it slides past posts, so small fingers can’t be trapped. The gate’s speed and the automatic closing delay are set with the school’s daily routine in mind, not left at the factory defaults.

Pedestrian gates are generally manual, with hydraulic self-closers and an electric lock. They should have anti-finger-trap hinges and a lock that holds firmly against a determined push. Under the Equality Act, the gate opening, the push buttons and the intercom need to work for wheelchair users and parents with buggies. That affects the gate width and the height at which controls are mounted.

The fencing and gates should match in height and design. School perimeters are typically 2.0 to 2.4 metres high, in weldmesh or vertical-bar railings with no climbable horizontal rails on the outside. Powder-coated finishes in the school’s colours are standard.

Linking to your existing systems

Many schools already have a visitor management system, CCTV or a door entry system on the main building. Gate intercoms and access control can often be linked to those, or managed from the same software, so the office has one screen for the gate and the front door. Whether that’s possible depends on the specific products. We check the exact model numbers at survey stage, rather than promising a link we haven’t confirmed.

Installation around the school year

Groundworks, ducting and gate installation are planned for half-terms and the summer holiday, so the site is never left without a secure perimeter while pupils are in. Larger projects are often phased over two holidays. Summer is the busiest time of year for school contractors, so getting in touch in spring gives you the most choice of dates.

Procurement and paperwork

We provide what schools, academy trusts and local authorities normally need: a site-specific risk assessment and method statement, insurance certificates, DBS checks for staff working on site, and drawings for approval. At handover you get operating instructions, staff training on daily use and emergency release, and the records your premises team needs. If you’re buying through a framework or need several quotes for your procurement rules, tell us at enquiry stage.

Cost of school gates and entrance security in London

As a rough guide, a powered sliding vehicle gate for a school entrance typically costs £8,000 to £20,000 installed, depending on width, groundworks and access control. A controlled pedestrian gate with an electric lock, self-closer and video intercom is usually £3,000 to £7,000. Airlock entrances, new perimeter fencing and links to existing systems are priced after survey. Every quote is itemised and fixed in writing.

Maintenance

Powered gates on a school site should be serviced at least every six months. That means a full safety check, force testing, adjustment and a written record each visit. HSE guidance on powered gates makes clear that whoever controls the site is responsible for keeping them safe. Between services, the premises team should check daily that the safety devices work and that nothing is damaged. We show them what to look for at handover. For existing gates that are faulty or out of service, see gate repair and servicing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the gate connect to our existing visitor system or CCTV?+
Often, yes, but it depends on the exact products. Send us the make and model of your current system and we’ll confirm what can link to it before it goes into the quote.
Should our vehicle gate be swing or sliding?+
Sliding in most cases, because it doesn’t swing out across the pavement or playground and needs less clear space. Swing gates can suit narrow entrances away from pedestrian routes.
What happens if the gate breaks down during the school day?+
Your premises team will be shown how to make the gate safe and open or lock it by hand. Response times for call-outs are set out in writing in the service agreement.
Can you replace just the gate and keep our fencing?+
Usually. We check the condition of the existing posts and fencing at survey and tell you if anything needs strengthening to carry a powered gate.
Do we need planning permission?+
Schools often have permitted development rights for gates and fencing, but height limits, conservation areas and listed buildings can change that. Our borough planning guides are a starting point, and we can advise on your site.

Also see our other commercial entrance options, and our borough planning guides.

Home/Guides/Aluminium vs Wooden Driveway Gates
Updated 13 October 2026

Aluminium vs Wooden Driveway Gates

Compare timber, painted aluminium and wood-effect finishes by appearance, construction, upkeep and complete installation scope.

On this page +
Compare samples at your propertyLook beyond the face of the gatePlan the upkeep you will acceptCompare equivalent quotationsA practical material comparisonChoose the board pattern before deciding on colourConstruction matters as much as the surfaceBudget for the upkeep you can realistically provideCompare three choices using the same entrance briefAsk what happens after accidental damage

Compare samples at your property

Timber has natural grain and variation; painted aluminium gives a more uniform surface. Wood-effect aluminium offers a printed or applied timber appearance, but grain repetition, edges and the rear face can look different from real wood.

View samples beside your brickwork in daylight and shade. Ask to see the finish on a corner, joint and reverse face, rather than choosing from a small photograph. Check how the posts, pedestrian gate and fencing will match.

Look beyond the face of the gate

For timber, ask for the species or modified-wood product, board construction, frame joints and finish specification. For aluminium, ask about the frame, infill, joints, coating and repair options. The material name alone does not establish stiffness, durability or suitability for automation.

Solid boards and open bars create different privacy and wind-exposure conditions. Discuss weight, dimensions, supports and movement with the installer. Compare the complete gate design instead of assuming that one material will suit every opening.

Plan the upkeep you will accept

Timber coatings need care appropriate to the species, exposure and selected finish. Ask how to recognise when attention is due and whether you want the wood to retain its original colour. Aluminium still needs the specified cleaning, coating checks and maintenance of its fittings.

Separate the timber or coating warranty from the gate fabrication, installation and automation terms. Ask about exclusions, maintenance records and labour charges. A raw-material warranty does not promise that the complete gate will remain unchanged for that period.

Compare equivalent quotations

Put the same opening dimensions, infill, finish, supports, automation and access controls into both quotations. Include removal of the old entrance, power, groundworks, VAT and reinstatement. This gives you a useful comparison without relying on a universal lifespan or percentage saving.

Explore wooden driveway gates and aluminium gates. For modified timber, read our Accoya guide and ask for the proposed product terms. Then discuss your entrance.

A practical material comparison

DecisionTimberAluminium
AppearanceNatural grain and variation, with the chosen species, board pattern and finish.Painted or wood-effect finish, with profiles and joints that vary by range.
ConstructionAsk about the frame, joints, board fixing, moisture management and fittings.Ask about frame sections, infill attachment, joints, coating and fittings.
CareObtain the specified cleaning and coating care for the wood and exposure.Obtain cleaning, coating inspection and hardware care instructions.
Damage and repairsAsk how damaged boards, joints and finishes could be repaired.Ask whether panels can be replaced and how finish repairs are handled.
AutomationAssess the complete gate, dimensions, supports and operating geometry.Apply the same complete-system assessment to the proposed design.
WarrantySeparate timber, fabrication, finish, fittings and installation terms.Separate coating, fabrication, fittings and installation terms.

Use the matrix to compare actual products. The terms wooden and aluminium cover many constructions and finishes. Neither material name gives a reliable installed price, security rating or guaranteed service life for the complete entrance.

Choose the board pattern before deciding on colour

A full boarded surface, spaced slats and an open upper section give different views through the entrance. Look from the pavement towards the house and from the house towards approaching visitors. Decide what needs screening and where visibility remains useful. Compare the rear face too, because that is the view you may see most often.

Ask for a drawing showing board widths, spacing, frame edges and the relationship between the driveway gate and any pedestrian gate. A narrow side gate may use a different arrangement of boards even when the finish matches. Check whether those differences are acceptable before fabrication.

For wood-effect aluminium, request a sample large enough to reveal repeating grain and the treatment of corners and ends. For timber, ask what variation to expect between boards and what the selected finish will look like after weathering. A small online colour swatch cannot settle those decisions.

For a period property, start with its actual boundary details rather than a rule that every older house must have timber or ornate metalwork. Where controls apply, discuss the proposed material and appearance with the relevant adviser before ordering. A convincing timber effect does not itself establish planning acceptability.

Construction matters as much as the surface

Ask the fabricator to explain how the frame supports the infill and where the hinges or running gear attach. Request the details that matter for your chosen width and height. If automation is proposed, have the gate supplier and installer agree the arrangement instead of treating a motor kit as an unrelated addition.

Discuss solid infill and wind exposure together. A gate made from a lighter material still presents a surface to the wind, and the supports and equipment need assessment for the actual design. Avoid substituting an assumed material advantage for a measured specification.

Look for a written approach to drainage and moisture around joints, board ends and fittings. Ask how the selected hardware suits the material and exterior location. These questions help compare the proposed workmanship without assuming that every gate from one material has the same construction.

If you want to keep existing posts or brick piers, include their assessment in both material quotations. A change of leaf material does not establish that the old supports or hinges are suitable for the new entrance.

Budget for the upkeep you can realistically provide

Ask each supplier for a care sheet before you accept the quotation. It should identify the permitted cleaning products, coating inspections and any specialist work. Consider access to both faces of the gate, nearby planting and the time or contractor help you are willing to allow for upkeep.

Decide whether you want timber to retain a particular colour or are comfortable with the appearance allowed by the chosen finish system. Record that preference when discussing coatings. Do not rely on a universal recoating interval taken from another species, finish or exposure.

For a coated aluminium gate, ask how to deal with a scratch, damaged edge or impact. Establish whether the supplier offers repair materials, replacement boards or a refinishing service, and request terms rather than assuming those services are included. Hardware and automation still require their own care.

For both materials, keep cleaning and service records where the terms require them. Ask who deals with a problem involving more than one supplier, such as movement that damages a finish. A long material warranty and a practical route to resolving an installation problem are different things.

Compare three choices using the same entrance brief

If your priority is natural grain and you accept the specified care, compare suitable timber constructions and finishes. Ask about species or modified timber by name and request a sample of the proposed product. Include the fabrication and coating scope so the choice is more precise than wood versus metal.

If you prefer a uniform painted appearance, compare aluminium ranges against a painted timber alternative. Keep the infill, opening layout and finish colour consistent. Ask what changes at the joints, frame edges and reverse face; those details can explain why two apparently similar gates look different in person.

If you want a timber appearance with a different care routine, put wood-effect aluminium beside a real timber sample at the property. Make the decision in daylight and shade. Check the proposed posts and pedestrian gate at the same time so you are comparing a complete frontage.

Write down the non-negotiable requirements before requesting prices: usable opening, privacy, pedestrian access, acceptable upkeep and operation. Then compare the complete installed cost and written terms. You can choose on those practical differences without relying on invented lifespan figures or promises that any material needs no maintenance.

Ask what happens after accidental damage

Consider a vehicle scraping one panel or a fitting being damaged during building work. Ask whether an individual component can be replaced, whether the original finish can be matched and who would carry out the repair. Availability and matching depend on the actual product, so request a supported repair route rather than a guarantee that a later replacement will be invisible.

Keep the approved drawing, colour reference, sample details and invoice. These records help a repair contractor identify the supplied gate and give you a clearer comparison if you later replace a pedestrian gate or extend the adjoining fence.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is aluminium maintenance-free?+
No. Follow the cleaning and inspection instructions for the finish, hardware and automation.
Does wood-effect aluminium look identical to timber?+
Compare full-size samples, joints and both faces in your own lighting. Finish systems differ and appearance is a personal choice.

Updated 13 October 2026

The Cost of Automating Existing Driveway Gates

Build a retrofit budget that includes the gate assessment, supports, power, controls and completed-system checks.

On this page +
Check whether the existing gate can be automatedSeparate the quotation into work packagesSpecify operation and handoverCompare retrofit and replacementCompare surface-mounted and underground operatorsIdentify what a motor kit actually includesPower routes and driveway work can change the budgetUse a quotation worksheet instead of a generic price bandThree retrofit scopes to discuss with the installerAgree the changeover day

Check whether the existing gate can be automated

Start with the gate and supports, before choosing a motor kit. The survey should assess condition, hinges or running gear, movement, dimensions, exposure to wind and hazards around the opening. A manual gate that can be pushed by hand is not automatically ready for powered operation.

Ask whether the proposal needs repairs, altered supports, a different opening arrangement or replacement leaves. Include that work in the comparison with a new gate.

Separate the quotation into work packages

Request separate descriptions for gate repairs, motor and controls, power supply, cable routes, groundworks and surface reinstatement. Include access equipment, protective measures and any work by other trades.

Record VAT, removal and disposal, appointments, permissions and exclusions. A kit price covers a different scope from an installed and checked entrance. The cheapest motor listing cannot establish the completed project cost.

Specify operation and handover

Explain how often the gate operates, who uses it and whether you need pedestrian access, delivery entry or an intercom. Ask for the proposed product models and the basis for choosing them.

The quotation should identify completed-system checks, documentation, user instruction and manual-release training. Confirm maintenance, repair support and the separate equipment and installation warranty terms in writing.

Compare retrofit and replacement

If repair and alteration costs are substantial, request a replacement option with equivalent appearance and controls. Compare the complete scope, disruption and upkeep rather than assuming retrofit must be cheaper.

Use the installed gate cost guide alongside our gate automation service. Send photographs, approximate dimensions and known faults when you discuss your entrance.

Further reading: HSE guidance on complete-system assessment.

Compare surface-mounted and underground operators

The operator type affects both the appearance of the gate and the installation work. Compare an above-ground linear or articulated-arm proposal with an underground proposal using the actual hinge and support arrangement. Ask for a drawing showing mounting positions, movement and access for servicing. Product names alone do not establish that either arrangement will fit.

OptionWork to establishQuestions for the quotation
Above-ground linear armMounting geometry on the leaf and support, brackets, cable route and movement clearance.Can suitable fixings be made to the existing structure, and what alterations are included?
Above-ground articulated armSpace for the linked arm and suitable mounting on the support and gate.Where does the mechanism move, and how will the surrounding area be assessed?
Underground operatorFoundation box, hinge relationship, excavation, drainage, cables and access to covers.Who provides drainage and reinstates the driveway, and what remains visible?
Existing sliding gate driveCondition of the gate, running gear, supports and compatible drive arrangement.Which existing parts can remain and what needs repair before automation?

Above-ground equipment can still require groundworks for supports or cables. Underground equipment can still leave covers and release fittings visible. Compare the documented site work rather than treating one option as excavation-free or the other as completely invisible.

Identify what a motor kit actually includes

Ask for a component list tied to the supplier and model numbers. Depending on the offer, a kit may include operators, a controller, receivers or selected accessories. It may exclude the equipment and work needed to make your particular entrance suitable. Have the installer mark supplied, retained and separately priced items on the same list.

A pair of existing manual gates also needs consideration as a structure and as a moving entrance. Photograph the hinges, supports and gate from safe positions, and send the approximate leaf dimensions. Tell the contractor about sagging, rubbing, repairs or occasions when wind moved a leaf unexpectedly.

Do not use a catalogue maximum weight as the only selection rule. Ask the contractor how the proposed equipment suits the gate dimensions, mounting geometry, infill, exposure and operating demand. The answer should identify the equipment being priced, not just promise a powerful motor.

Power routes and driveway work can change the budget

Draw the approximate route from the entrance towards the available supply and flag finished paving, steps, walls, trees and inspection covers along it. The electrician and gate installer need to establish the actual electrical requirements and cable route. A photograph can help an initial discussion but cannot confirm the condition or suitability of the supply.

If you plan a new driveway, agree ducts, foundations and finished levels before the paving programme starts. Name who provides each part of the work and who checks the interfaces between trades. Include making good even where an existing route may be reusable; the quote should say what happens if inspection finds that it cannot be used.

For underground operators, request a specific drainage proposal for the site. Ask how covers remain accessible after resurfacing and how future equipment replacement would be approached. These are ownership questions as well as installation costs, because the cheapest initial arrangement may be inconvenient to maintain.

Use a quotation worksheet instead of a generic price band

Create one row for each work package and one column for each proposal. Copy the contractor’s description and price into the worksheet without converting an allowance into a fixed amount. Leave an item marked not stated until the contractor clarifies it. That makes omissions visible before a deposit is agreed.

Separate the base installation from choices such as a different intercom, extra remotes or an additional pedestrian entrance. Record ongoing charges beside the features they support. A smartphone option may involve different ownership and connectivity arrangements from a fixed indoor answering point.

Check payment stages, quotation validity, VAT treatment and how variations require approval. Ask what happens if concealed damage or unsuitable foundations emerge after work starts. Avoid assuming an advertised equipment price includes fitting, electrical work, disposal or complete-system checks.

Where two proposals differ materially, ask for a comparable alternative rather than negotiating an unexplained total. A contractor who includes replacing damaged supports is pricing a different job from one who assumes that the existing supports can remain.

Three retrofit scopes to discuss with the installer

For sound gates with suitable supports, the main question may be the operator arrangement and the work needed to connect, protect and commission the entrance. Ask the installer to confirm the condition and list retained components. Treat this as a possible scope, not an assurance that your own manual gates are ready.

For gates that sag or scrape, separate the repair proposal from automation. Ask what the repair would achieve, how the result would be assessed and whether further alterations remain necessary. A motor should not become the explanation for forcing a poorly moving gate through its travel.

For an entrance that needs major support work and new controls, compare a complete replacement using an equivalent design brief. Retaining the leaves may still be worthwhile for appearance or conservation reasons, but the quotation should show the cost and limitations of that choice.

These examples explain why a useful budget begins with a scope. Once the contractor has surveyed your gate, request a written proposal you can compare against the alternative, with the same finish, controls, safe operation and handover requirements.

Agree the changeover day

Ask how long the entrance is expected to be unavailable and where vehicles should be parked during the work. Confirm access for residents, pedestrians and deliveries, especially if the gate is the only entrance. Programme electrical and driveway work around the installation rather than leaving responsibility unclear between contractors.

Before paying the final balance under your agreed terms, request the documented checks, user instructions and demonstration included in the quotation. Identify who will deal with any incomplete item and when it is expected to be resolved. Keep model numbers, settings records supplied for the owner and warranty documents together.

If the installer discovers work outside the agreed scope, request the reason, revised price and effect on the programme before authorising it. That is more useful than trying to compare an unexpectedly enlarged retrofit with an earlier equipment-only estimate.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you give a fixed retrofit price from a motor model?+
A motor model does not identify the repairs, power, groundworks or protective measures needed. A site assessment establishes the complete scope.
Can I keep my existing controls?+
Compatibility and condition need checking against the proposed equipment. Identify retained parts and any limitations in the quotation.

Home/Guides/Choosing an Intercom for Your Driveway Gate
Updated 13 October 2026

Choosing an Intercom for Your Driveway Gate

Compare audio, video, wired, IP and GSM gate intercoms, including retrofit compatibility, smartphone access, installation costs and handover checks.

On this page +
Decide where you want to answer visitorsAudio or video: choose the visitor information you needWired, IP and mobile intercoms: compare the whole routeCompare the connection pathsSmartphone apps and smart-home integrationRetrofit an intercom without replacing the whole entranceGet the exact equipment and account termsCompare installation costs and ongoing commitmentsShared entrances, recordings and control of accountsPlan installation and supportA handover demonstration worth asking for

Decide where you want to answer visitors

List who should receive a call and whether they need an indoor monitor, phone calls, an app or a combination. Include anyone who does not use a smartphone. Decide what happens if nobody answers and how a visitor can leave a delivery.

Ask for a demonstration of the actual sequence: call, identify the visitor, grant entry and confirm that the gate has finished moving. Seeing a video does not necessarily mean the app reports the gate’s physical position.

Place the intercom decision within your driveway and home security plan, so identifying callers, controlling entry and protecting parked vehicles work together.

Audio or video: choose the visitor information you need

An audio intercom lets you speak to the visitor. A video intercom adds a view from its camera. Decide whether a conversation is enough for your entrance or whether you need to see a caller before granting access. Consider household members who find a small screen, quiet speaker or app notification difficult to use.

For video, ask to see the view from the proposed mounting position. A camera aimed at a driver may not give the same view of someone on foot. Discuss lighting after dark, glare, weather exposure and the position of a caller using a wheelchair. A specification such as camera resolution cannot answer those layout questions.

Decide whether you want live viewing only or recordings, missed-call images and notifications. Have the supplier identify which features the proposed configuration provides and any storage or subscription requirements. Avoid assuming that video entry automatically includes recording or confirms the position of the gate.

Wired, IP and mobile intercoms: compare the whole route

Separate the connection between gate and house from the method used to answer a call. A system can have wired components and still use an app for some functions. Conversely, a wireless call path does not remove the need to supply and connect the equipment at the entrance.

OptionWhen to consider itConfirm before ordering
Dedicated wired indoor answeringYou want a fixed handset or monitor for use at home.Cable condition and route, compatible indoor units and whether local calls need any network service.
IP or app-based answeringYou want supported network features or calls on selected phones.Network coverage, account ownership, app support and which functions depend on an internet or cloud service.
Mobile-network entryA suitable cellular service offers a practical call path at the entrance.Device and SIM compatibility, voice or data requirements, signal and recurring charges.

Some products combine indoor answering with phone access. Have the installer explain the configuration, including what still works if one connection fails. Calling a system hardwired does not establish that all of its features operate without the internet.

Compare the connection paths

A wired indoor system can suit a household that wants a dedicated answering point. An IP system needs the specified network and power arrangements. A mobile-network intercom needs suitable coverage, device support and a compatible SIM plan.

Test the connection at the proposed gate position. A strong indoor Wi-Fi signal or a phone signal from another network does not prove the intercom will work there. Discuss what remains available during a broadband, mobile-service or power failure.

Smartphone apps and smart-home integration

Write down the devices your household uses and the actions you need: answer a visitor, view the entrance, request opening or receive a missed-call notification. Ask the installer to demonstrate those actions on the proposed equipment. Support for one action does not establish support for all the others.

The Comelit app documentation, for example, lists entrance-panel calls and gate release among its functions, with manuals for named video-entry devices. Ask which functions the quoted hardware supports. That is why a brand name or an app logo is not enough to confirm compatibility with an existing installation.

For Ring, Google Home, Control4 or another existing system, use our smart-home integration checklist to define the exact functions and equipment. Confirm who supports the connection after an update and how account access transfers when you change phone or sell the property. Do not assume a general-purpose video doorbell includes a supported gate-release interface.

Retrofit an intercom without replacing the whole entrance

Start with the controller, existing answering equipment and any cable records. Ask the contractor to inspect the available route, supply and release connection. Reusing a cable or indoor monitor may be possible with a compatible system, but the proposal should identify the equipment it intends to keep and any limitations.

Tell the contractor whether you need full vehicle entry, pedestrian access or a separate pedestrian gate. Describe how each entrance should respond rather than asking for an extra relay without explaining its purpose. The team needs to assess the command interface alongside the safe operation of the gates.

If the current intercom rings but the gate does not open, record that symptom before deciding to replace the intercom. The calling function and release function need separate assessment. Buying a new entrance panel may not resolve a fault elsewhere in the system. This buying guide cannot diagnose that fault from the ringing sound alone.

Get the exact equipment and account terms

Request model numbers, the proposed release interface, supported monitors and app requirements. Confirm recording options, retention, subscriptions, SIM charges and which account owns the system. Ask how to remove a former resident or contractor.

Product families contain different devices. Compare named configurations rather than assuming a brand guarantees compatibility. Our Comelit and Hikvision comparison shows why the component list matters.

Compare installation costs and ongoing commitments

A useful quotation names the entrance panel, camera if required, indoor answering devices, power equipment and connection to the gate. It also describes cable work, mounting, network setup, configuration, testing and reinstatement. Ask whether VAT is included and which items depend on the site survey.

Compare recurring costs on the same basis. List SIM charges, subscriptions, recording or cloud-storage plans and any paid support. Confirm what happens to each function if a subscription ends. Ask the supplier to distinguish equipment warranty from installation workmanship and explain how future visits will be charged.

There is no sound universal fitted price for every London entrance. An existing usable cable route and a new route through finished paving involve different work. For a meaningful comparison, send each contractor the same brief and request the same answering points and access functions, rather than comparing only the price of the outdoor panel.

Shared entrances, recordings and control of accounts

For flats or a shared driveway, specify which household receives each call and who manages changes when residents move. Ask how visitors find the right name and how delivery access will work. Confirm the proposed capacity, user permissions and any management charges for the particular configuration.

If recording is proposed, discuss the camera view, whether audio is recorded, who can view footage, where it is stored and how long it is retained. Avoid treating a camera as permission to record neighbouring property without considering privacy. Agree the appropriate arrangements for the actual site before enabling recording.

Keep the property owner or responsible managing agent in control of administrator access and recovery details. Ask for a demonstration of removing a former resident without disrupting everyone else. Include residents who prefer a fixed answering point or cannot rely on a smartphone in the requirements from the start.

Plan installation and support

Include cable routes, power, camera position, lighting, accessibility and weather exposure in the survey. Confirm who commissions the connection to the gate controller and checks operation of the complete entrance.

Compare video intercoms and phone entry. Check Ofcom’s network-retirement guidance before buying mobile-network equipment.

A handover demonstration worth asking for

Use the visitor journey to check the installation with the contractor: a person arrives at the intended calling position, selects the right household, makes contact and receives a response. Then confirm the authorised release action and how users should observe or verify the entrance. Keep people outside the movement area during the demonstration.

  • Check conversation quality and, where fitted, the camera view in the agreed conditions.
  • Demonstrate calls to each specified monitor or phone, including the unanswered-call arrangement.
  • Explain which functions depend on power, broadband, mobile service or an active account.
  • Show user management and provide the correct equipment instructions.
  • Record support contacts, renewal responsibilities and the agreed fallback access.

A successful video call does not prove the whole powered gate is safe. The installer needs to check the completed entrance and its protective measures. Ask for the handover records and maintenance advice, and keep them accessible to the person responsible for the property.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which brand is best?+
Compare the proposed models against your wiring, visitor workflow, network, account costs and support requirements. A brand ranking cannot establish compatibility.
Does an app continue working during a power cut?+
That depends on backup power for the gate, intercom and network equipment, as well as the service connection. Ask for the actual failure arrangements.
Can I keep an indoor monitor and answer on my phone?+
Some compatible configurations provide both. Ask for the exact monitor, network or gateway equipment, app requirements and unanswered-call behaviour rather than assuming every product in a range supports them.
Can an intercom be fitted to my existing gates?+
A contractor needs to assess the gate controller, command interface, power and cable arrangements. Existing components may be reusable, but a universal retrofit promise would not establish compatibility.
Will a video intercom show whether the gate is closed?+
A camera view and a gate-position signal are different features. Ask how the proposed system establishes and displays the actual gate state; do not assume an opening command confirms movement.

Pricing & CostsUpdated 6 November 2026

Electric Driveway Gate Costs in London

Compare the full cost of an electric driveway gate, from supply and groundworks to power, access controls and ongoing care.

On this page +
Start with the complete installed costTypical installed price ranges in LondonThe items to include in your quotationHow gate material and opening layout affect the priceGroundworks, electrical supply and making goodNew installation and retrofit: two different scopesVAT, exclusions and payment stagesBudget for ownership as well as installationPrepare an enquiry that helps us quote

The cost of electric driveway gates depends on the entrance as well as the gate. A supply-only price leaves out work such as supports, electrical supply and installation. To set a useful budget, ask for a measured survey and an itemised quotation covering the complete job.

Start with the complete installed cost

A gate advertised at a particular price may include only the leaves or sliding panel. A motor-kit price may cover the motor and controller without the work needed to make the complete installation suitable for your site. Before comparing totals, establish whether each quotation covers the same opening, materials and work.

There is no single installed price that applies to every London driveway. Width and height, ground conditions, access for the installation team, existing pillars, the power route and your chosen entry controls can change the scope. A useful quotation identifies those items and states what remains subject to inspection.

For a new powered entrance, discuss a complete automated gate installation. For gates you intend to keep, start with an assessment for automating existing gates. The two projects need different quotations.

Typical installed price ranges in London

These guide ranges come from our current pricing for complete jobs. They are not quotes. Your price depends on the measured entrance, supports, groundworks and power route, and is confirmed in an itemised written quote after a free site survey. Check whether VAT is included, as explained below.

Time on site covers the installation visit once the gates are made. Fabrication lead time is separate and depends on the design. To start a project, see how we design, supply and install driveway gates in London, or browse every gate type we install.

The items to include in your quotation

Part of the jobAsk the quotation to identify
Gate supplyDimensions, material, construction, finish, delivery and fittings.
Supports and groundworksPosts or pillar alterations, foundations, track or other support work, drainage and removal of waste.
AutomationMotor and controller models, installation, system-specific protective measures and commissioning.
Electrical workSupply assessment, cable route, required work and who provides the relevant test records.
Access controlsRemotes, intercom, keypad or phone entry, connectivity and ongoing charges.
Finishing and handoverReinstatement of paving or planting, removal of old equipment, user instructions and demonstration.
Price and termsVAT treatment, exclusions, allowances, payment stages, warranty and maintenance conditions.

Ask who supplies each item and who takes responsibility for the assembled installation. If separate trades are involved, agree the handover between them before work starts.

How gate material and opening layout affect the price

Compare the specified product rather than assuming one material will always cost less. Aluminium gates vary in profile construction and finish. Composite gates need a defined board-and-frame specification. With hardwood gates, the timber, joinery and coating affect the work and future care.

Bespoke dimensions and decorative fabrication can change the cost of a gate. Request the drawing and finish reference that match the price. Include the posts, hinges, locks and visible hardware in the comparison.

Swing and sliding layouts involve different support and movement arrangements. A sliding quotation needs the proposed track or cantilever support and space along the boundary. A swing quotation needs adequate movement space and suitable supports. Let the measured layout guide the choice, then compare the cost of suitable options.

Groundworks, electrical supply and making good

Ask the surveyor to trace the proposed power route and identify the surfaces that need to be lifted. A short route across a planted border and a route beneath finished paving involve different work. Agree who reinstates those surfaces and whether the quote includes matching materials or an allowance.

Existing pillars and foundations may need investigation before the installer can confirm that they are suitable. Discuss access for equipment, waste removal and any arrangements affecting neighbours or a shared driveway. Request a process for agreeing extra work if the team finds an issue after excavation.

Check planning or other permissions before committing to the work. Ask the relevant local authority about your particular boundary where restrictions may apply, and include any application or professional costs in your own budget. A contractor’s gate quotation does not automatically include these expenses.

New installation and retrofit: two different scopes

The following are scope comparisons, not completed projects or quoted prices.

A new gate and automated entrance

Compare gate supply, new or adapted supports, groundworks, power, motors, controls and finishing as one project. Ask which parts of the work the named contractor will complete and which require another trade. A low gate-supply figure does not establish the final installed total.

Automation added to existing gates

Ask the installer to assess the condition, movement and supports of the retained gates before pricing the motors. Repairs, altered hinges, new supports or other changes may be needed. The quotation should say which parts remain, which change and how the completed system will be assessed and handed over.

HSE’s powered-gate safety guidance explains why the gate, equipment and site need consideration together. Keep protective measures and commissioning in the scope when comparing prices.

VAT, exclusions and payment stages

Ask for the amount payable, whether it includes VAT and the basis for any exception. GOV.UK states that most building work on homes attracts the standard 20% rate, with exceptions. That does not establish the VAT status of an individual supplier or the treatment of your project; get both confirmed on the quotation.

Check whether quoted sums are fixed items or allowances that can change once details are known. Ask the contractor to list exclusions such as power work, old-gate disposal, replacement paving, permits or subscriptions. Agree how variations need your approval.

Keep the payment schedule with the specification. Confirm what each stage covers, the expected lead time and the arrangements if the scope or delivery date changes. If you consider finance from any provider, compare the total repayable and fees; this guide does not assume that gate finance is available from us.

Budget for ownership as well as installation

Keep separate lines for electricity, servicing, connectivity subscriptions and repairs. Ask for the installed equipment’s maintenance instructions and the proposed service scope. Visit charges, replacement parts and labour outside a service agreement can affect your later spending.

For electricity, obtain the standby power, operating demand and expected usage for the proposed equipment. Energy in kWh equals power in watts divided by 1,000, multiplied by hours of use. Calculate standby and active use separately and apply your own tariff without counting the same operating time twice. Include intercoms and other powered accessories if their demand is separate.

For a chosen ownership period, add installation, electricity, service visits, subscription charges and any repair allowances. Treat repair allowances as your planning assumptions rather than predictions. There is no reliable single annual cost for all gate systems.

Ask what each warranty covers, whether it includes labour and the conditions for making a claim. Gate material, coating, motors and workmanship may have different terms. Do not assume insurance discounts, resale gains or savings from a new system; check any relevant policy with your insurer and compare actual quotations. If an existing system is unreliable, request a repair assessment before deciding to replace it.

Prepare an enquiry that helps us quote

Send your area or postcode, photographs from both sides of the entrance and a description of how you want to use it. Include approximate dimensions if you have them, the current gate type, any known power supply and whether you want a pedestrian entrance. A survey is still needed to establish the final specification.

Tell us which matters most to you: privacy, appearance, vehicle access or easier daily use. Mention a budget if you have one so we can discuss the scope before developing a proposal.

Request a gate quotation and ask for the items above in writing. Keep the quotation, drawing, agreed changes, handover documents and maintenance instructions together for future reference.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much do electric driveway gates cost installed in London?+
As a guide, fully installed electric sliding gates typically cost £4,500 to £12,000 and electric swing gates £3,500 to £10,000. Automating existing gates is typically £1,200 to £3,500. The total depends on the measured entrance, gate specification, supports, groundworks, power and controls, and is confirmed in an itemised quotation after a site survey. A gate-only or motor-kit price is not a complete installed price.
Is automating existing gates cheaper than replacing them?+
It depends on what can be retained. An assessment may identify repairs or changes to the gate and supports before automation. Compare a written retrofit scope with a replacement quotation rather than assuming that keeping the leaves makes the whole job cheaper.
Should the quote include VAT?+
Ask the supplier to state whether VAT applies, the rate used and the final amount payable. Do not compare a VAT-exclusive figure with an inclusive total.
What ongoing costs should I allow for?+
Allow for electricity, maintenance, any connectivity subscriptions and repairs outside warranty or service cover. Use the proposed equipment details, your tariff and written service terms instead of a generic annual estimate.
Can you give a price from photographs?+
Photographs and approximate dimensions help us understand the enquiry. The measured opening, supports, power route and proposed scope still need assessment before a final quotation.
