Electric Gate Running Costs: Calculate Your Electricity Use

Estimate annual gate electricity use from movement time, standby demand and your own electricity tariff.

On this page +
Measure two different loadsA worked example with explicit unitsAdapt the calculation to your gateElectricity is only part of ownership costCompare running costs without confusing voltage and consumption

Measure two different loads

A gate uses electricity while moving and may also draw power while waiting. The controller, intercom, access receiver, network equipment and battery charger can contribute to that waiting load. Motor output ratings alone do not give the electricity drawn by the complete entrance.

Ask for measured input power or manufacturer consumption figures for the specified equipment. For two motors, use the combined demand. Record the total powered movement time for opening and closing, rather than treating an opening as a complete cycle.

A worked example with explicit units

This is an illustration, not a typical installation or a current tariff quote. Assume the complete system draws 100 W while moving and 5 W while idle. It makes ten complete cycles per day, each with 20 seconds of total powered movement.

Annual movement time = 20 × 10 × 365 ÷ 3,600 = 20.28 hours. Movement electricity = 0.100 kW × 20.28 hours = 2.03 kWh.

A 365-day year contains 8,760 hours. Idle time = 8,760 − 20.28 = 8,739.72 hours. Idle electricity = 0.005 kW × 8,739.72 hours = 43.70 kWh. Total electricity = 45.73 kWh. At an example tariff of £0.30 per kWh, that is £13.72 per year.

Adapt the calculation to your gate

Use annual kWh = (moving watts × moving hours + idle watts × idle hours) ÷ 1,000. Multiply the result by your unit tariff in pounds per kWh. Use 8,784 hours for a leap year.

The example treats moving power as the whole system demand during movement, so it subtracts movement time from idle time. If your motor figure is an additional load above a separately measured continuous baseline, calculate that baseline over the whole year instead. Do not count the same load twice.

If a cycle takes 40 seconds instead of 20, change the movement time before calculating both parts. Heaters, lighting and accessories that switch separately need their own power-and-time calculations.

Electricity is only part of ownership cost

SIM plans, cloud subscriptions, servicing, replacement batteries and repairs are separate costs. Ask which apply to the proposed equipment and whether VAT is included. An existing household electricity standing charge is not usually an additional gate cost; a separate metered supply could introduce one.

Keep electricity estimates separate from maintenance budgets when using our installed gate cost guide. For a retrofit, compare the work described in our automation quotation guide.

Compare running costs without confusing voltage and consumption

A label such as 24 V describes a voltage, not the annual electricity bill. Compare the input energy used by the complete installation and its actual operating pattern. If you are replacing equipment, ask whether the quoted consumption includes the controller, receiver, intercom and any backup charging.

Keep fixed ownership costs separate from electricity. A useful annual worksheet has distinct lines for energy, scheduled maintenance, connectivity or app services, and a repair allowance chosen for your own budget. Mark which amounts are quotations and which are assumptions. Do not turn a small calculated electricity cost into a claim that the entrance costs almost nothing to own.

If your household changes how it uses the gate, revise the cycle count and movement time in the example. If new always-on equipment is added, revise the idle demand too. Ask a competent person for suitable consumption information; do not open a control cabinet or insert an unsuitable measuring device to obtain it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is 100 W for 20 seconds, ten times a day, 20.3 kWh per year?+
No. Under those assumptions it is about 2.03 kWh per year. Standby and other equipment must be calculated separately.
Is the example my likely bill?+
No. Replace the sample power, operating time and tariff with figures for your own system.

Electric Gate Force Testing: What Homeowners Should Ask

Understand what force testing can show, how it fits into a gate safety assessment and which records to request from a competent engineer.

On this page +
What force testing measuresWhere testing fits into the safety assessmentWhy one force number is not enoughWhat to request in the reportWhen to arrange an assessmentLeave adjustments and powered tests to a competent personFAQs

What force testing measures

Force testing measures forces produced when a moving gate encounters a test instrument under specified conditions. An engineer uses the results to assess the relevant protection and to establish a record for later checks. A person pushing against the gate cannot provide an equivalent measurement.

The appropriate procedure depends on the gate, its movement and the protective approach used. This guide explains the questions to ask; it does not provide a test procedure or a set of universal pass values.

Where testing fits into the safety assessment

Force limitation is one possible part of a gate’s protective measures. Where the installation relies on it, the installer needs to verify its performance. Other risks can require different measures, and an acceptable reading at one test point does not establish that the whole entrance is safe.

The assessment also needs to consider trapping and shearing areas, access to moving parts, the people using the entrance and foreseeable behaviour. Read our guide to photocells, edges and loops to understand why devices have different roles.

Why one force number is not enough

Force limits and test methods relate to defined conditions, positions and time periods. Presenting a number as a continuous safe pressure, or assuming the same value applies at every edge, loses that context. Do not use a simplified web table to approve an installation.

Ask the engineer which current standard or other technical approach supports the assessment, which risks the tests address and how the results will be recorded. They should have the competence and equipment for the work. Changes to force or sensitivity settings should not be a homeowner troubleshooting step.

What to request in the report

Ask the report to identify the entrance and equipment, the date and person doing the work, the checks undertaken, any limitations, findings and required actions. Where force tests are relevant, request the recorded results and their assessment in context.

Keep these records with the user instructions and handover documents. A statement that the gate opens and closes is not a substitute for a safety assessment. If an unsafe condition is identified, ask how the entrance should be kept out of use and what must happen before it can operate again.

When to arrange an assessment

Arrange advice after damage, unexpected movement, a suspected failure of a protective function or a change to the gate or drive. Follow the checking arrangements specified for your system. The requirements for a business or rented property may differ from those of a privately owned domestic entrance.

See our responsibilities guide. Avoid treating a fixed annual date as either a complete safety guarantee or a universal statutory requirement for all private homeowners.

Leave adjustments and powered tests to a competent person

Do not test the closing force with your body, a pet, a vehicle or improvised objects. Keep people clear if you suspect a fault and follow the supplied instructions for taking the gate out of use, provided that can be done safely.

Request a gate assessment and agree the inspection scope before booking. Sources: HSE guidance on powered-gate safety and HSE guidance on responsibilities.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does one passing force reading mean the gate is safe?+
No. A reading relates to particular conditions and locations. The complete entrance and its other hazards and protective measures still need assessment.
Can I test a gate by pushing against it?+
No. Do not use a person or improvised obstruction as a force-test instrument. Ask a competent engineer to carry out the appropriate assessment with suitable equipment.
Do all powered gates use the same protection and test procedure?+
No. The gate, environment, foreseeable users and protective approach determine what must be assessed and verified. Where force limitation is used, its performance needs suitable verification.

Home/Guides/How to Manually Open an Electric Gate During a Power Cut
Updated 13 October 2026

How to Manually Open an Electric Gate During a Power Cut

Find the correct manual-release instructions for your gate and understand when to stop and ask for help instead of forcing it open.

On this page +
Start with the instructions supplied for your gateCheck whether releasing it could allow uncontrolled movementLocate the release without dismantling the operatorFollow the model-specific isolation and release sequenceBefore returning to automatic operationPrepare for the next power interruptionFAQs

Start with the instructions supplied for your gate

Manual release arrangements differ between operators. Find the user instructions for your installed system and the release training provided at handover. Check the model from records or an identification label only where you can see it safely.

This guide cannot supply a universal key direction, cover-opening sequence or release position. If the instructions or key are missing, contact the installer or a competent gate engineer before attempting to release the mechanism.

Prepare your fallback access arrangements as part of a wider driveway and home security plan, including keys, authorised users and the household’s response to a fault.

Check whether releasing it could allow uncontrolled movement

Keep people, pets and vehicles away from the gate’s movement area. A gate freed from its drive may move because of a slope, wind or its own weight. Damage to hinges, supports or running gear can make manual movement unsafe.

Do not release a leaning, derailed, damaged or unstable gate. If you cannot control and secure it using the supplied instructions, keep clear and seek assistance. If someone is trapped or faces immediate danger, call the emergency services.

Locate the release without dismantling the operator

A surface-mounted operator may have a release on its housing. An underground swing-gate system may use a release arrangement near the gate or foundation box. A sliding system may have a release associated with its operator. The exact location and access method depend on the product.

Use the manufacturer’s diagram for your model. Do not open electrical enclosures, remove guards or disconnect drive components to search for a release. A key from another system may not fit or operate it correctly.

Follow the model-specific isolation and release sequence

Follow the supplied instructions for isolating power and preventing automatic operation before release. A mains power cut does not establish that every part is unpowered: the installation may have a backup battery or another supply.

Only operate the release and move the gate if the instructions and conditions allow you to do so safely. Use the specified method of holding or securing it. Do not force a seized key, lever or gate. Stop if movement is uneven, unexpectedly heavy or uncontrolled.

Before returning to automatic operation

Use the manufacturer’s instructions for securing the gate, re-engaging the drive and restoring operation. Keep the movement area clear. If the original problem was a mechanical fault rather than a power cut, restoring the supply does not resolve it.

If you are unsure whether the mechanism has re-engaged or the gate behaves differently, stop using it and arrange an assessment. Do not bypass sensors or repeatedly trigger the motor to make it reconnect.

Prepare for the next power interruption

Keep the correct key accessible to authorised users and store the instructions where they can be found. Ask the installer to demonstrate release and explain when it must not be attempted. Agree how people can use the entrance during a fault.

Backup capacity depends on the product, battery condition, accessories and use. Ask for the actual specification rather than a fixed cycle count. For a stuck mechanism, request gate repair assistance. See HSE guidance on responsibilities for user information and release arrangements.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is the manual release on my gate?+
Check the user instructions for the exact operator. Surface, underground and sliding systems can have different release arrangements. Do not dismantle equipment to look for one.
What if I have lost the release key?+
Contact the installer or a gate engineer with the safely obtained equipment details. Do not force the lock or assume that another model’s key is suitable.
Will the gate work during a power cut?+
Only if the installed system has a suitable backup arrangement and it can support the required use. Runtime varies; check the actual specification and condition.
The gate is hard to move after release. Should I push harder?+
No. Stop, keep the area clear and ask for assistance. Resistance or uncontrolled movement can indicate a mechanical or structural problem.

Gate Safety Devices: Photocells, Safety Edges and Loops

Understand the different roles and limits of gate photocells, safety edges and vehicle loops, and why the whole entrance needs assessment.

On this page +
Start with the hazards at the entranceWhat photocells can detectWhat safety edges doWhat vehicle loops doPositioning and testing must suit the systemWhat owners should do when something changesFAQs

Start with the hazards at the entrance

Safety devices perform different functions. A gate can have several devices fitted and still present an unaddressed trapping or crushing risk. The installer needs to assess the complete gate, its movement, nearby structures and the people who may encounter it.

Ask the proposal to explain the risks identified and how the design addresses them. Do not treat a shopping list of sensors as a substitute for that assessment.

What photocells can detect

A photocell arrangement detects interruption of a beam or detection path. The area it covers depends on its design and positioning. A single beam does not detect every person or object anywhere around the gate.

The control system’s response depends on the equipment and configuration. Do not assume every beam interruption always causes the same stop or reversal in every operating direction. Ask the installer to explain the intended response and user checks.

What safety edges do

A suitable safety edge can detect contact along the area it protects and signal the control system. Selection, positioning, compatibility and the response of the complete system matter. Fitting an edge to one part of a gate does not establish protection at every other trapping point.

Ask which hazards the edges address and how their function will be verified. Damaged, loose or disconnected protection needs competent attention. Do not defeat a device to keep using the gate.

What vehicle loops do

An inductive loop detects a change caused by a suitable vehicle within its detection area. Depending on the design, it may form part of an access-control or vehicle-presence arrangement.

Do not rely on a vehicle loop to detect a pedestrian or provide all necessary protection. The installer must consider people on foot, cyclists, visitors and others alongside vehicle use. A convenient opening trigger and a safety function are not automatically interchangeable.

Positioning and testing must suit the system

There is no mounting height or device combination in this article that can approve every entrance. Gate geometry, surroundings, users and operating arrangements affect the specification. A competent installer needs to verify the proposed protective measures before handover.

Where force limitation is part of the protection, suitable verification is needed. Read our force-testing guide rather than attempting a test with your body or an improvised obstacle.

What owners should do when something changes

Follow the user instructions for routine checks and cleaning. Report visible damage, unexpected movement or a suspected failure of protection. Keep people clear and follow isolation instructions where you can do so safely.

Have a competent person assess faults and changes, including changes to the surrounding entrance. Keep records and ask when the gate can return to use. See HSE guidance on powered-gate safety, or request a gate assessment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will photocells detect everyone around a gate?+
No. Detection is limited to the arrangement’s coverage and operating conditions. Other hazards and people outside that area still need to be considered in the assessment.
Can a vehicle loop replace pedestrian protection?+
Do not assume that it can. A loop’s vehicle-detection function does not establish protection for people on foot. The complete entrance needs an appropriate safety assessment.
Can I bypass a faulty sensor temporarily?+
No. Stop using the affected system and obtain competent assistance. A bypass can remove protection that the installation relies on.

Updated 13 October 2026

Swing vs Sliding Driveway Gates

Compare parking clearance, side space, slopes and everyday access before choosing how your driveway gate opens.

On this page +
Measure the space each leaf occupiesAllow for the full sliding arrangementSlopes and drainage can change the choiceChoose around daily useCompare the layouts on the same drawingThree parking situations worth sketchingWind exposure, privacy and the gate designPlan walking access and breakdown arrangementsCompare installation and ownership costsBring these details to a survey

Measure the space each leaf occupies

A swing leaf travels around its hinge. For an illustrative pair of equal leaves across a 3.5 m opening, each leaf is about 1.75 m wide before allowing for gaps and fittings. Its free edge traces an arc with roughly that radius, rather than the full 3.5 m opening width.

That arithmetic is not a safe parking distance. Hinge position, opening angle, vehicle shape, pedestrian routes and protective clearances determine the usable space. Ask for a scaled plan showing the gate in motion and your car parked.

Allow for the full sliding arrangement

A sliding gate moves beside the entrance. The gate needs room along that path, including its supporting arrangement and safe separation from walls, fences and people. Cantilever designs have a supporting tail; tracked and multi-panel systems have different space requirements.

A car may be able to park beyond the sliding path, but the survey still needs to consider turning, waiting and pedestrian access. Read about telescopic options if side space is limited.

Slopes and drainage can change the choice

A rising driveway can obstruct a swing leaf. A sliding layout also needs a suitable travel path, supports and drainage. Neither layout becomes suitable simply by adding a stronger motor.

Share measured levels and any flooding history with the installer. Our sloping-driveway guide explains the questions to resolve before ordering.

Choose around daily use

Consider where visitors stop, how pedestrians enter, and how bins and deliveries pass the gate. Ask how you will operate the entrance during a power cut and what maintenance access the design needs.

Compare swing-gate installation with sliding-gate installation using the same design and access requirements. Groundworks and the complete specification determine cost; there is no fixed percentage difference that applies to every site.

Compare the layouts on the same drawing

Put both proposals on a plan showing the same opening, house, parking positions and boundary. Mark the gate closed, partway through its movement and fully open. Comparing only the open position can miss a conflict that occurs halfway through the cycle. Ask the surveyor to distinguish the structural opening from the clear space available to a vehicle after fittings and stops are installed.

QuestionSwing gatesSliding gates
Where does the gate go?Each leaf sweeps around its hinges into an agreed opening area.The panel travels sideways into a run-back area beside the entrance.
What must remain clear?The full arc, equipment and protective clearances, including when cars are parked.The whole travel path, supports, drive and protected run-back zone.
What site work matters?Suitable posts or piers, hinge geometry, levels and operator mounting.Suitable foundations and guides, plus the specified track or cantilever support.
What can make it awkward?A short parking bay, rising ground or a walking route through the swept area.A return wall, bin store, tree or another entrance occupying the storage side.
What should the quote show?Leaf sizes, opening direction, operator type and complete site work.Panel length, stored position, support design and complete site work.

Neither column supplies a minimum clearance. Use the table to identify the measurements that are missing from your quotation. A design that fits on an empty plan still needs checking against the way people actually use the property.

Three parking situations worth sketching

For a short driveway with parking straight ahead, show the rear or front of the car nearest the gate, including a tow bar or other projection. A swing layout may work if the vehicle can park beyond the complete swept area; a sliding layout may be worth comparing if that position is impractical. Do not turn the illustrative leaf-radius calculation into a parking instruction.

For two cars parked side by side, draw both vehicles and their doors open. A gate that avoids one car can still obstruct access beside the other. Show how somebody gets from each parking space to the front door without stepping into the moving gate area. Include the position used when unloading shopping or helping a child out.

For a narrow approach or tight turn, include the vehicle arriving from the street as well as its final parking position. A wider gate opening may help one part of the manoeuvre while leaving another corner constrained. Ask the surveyor to assess your actual vehicle and approach; a catalogue gate width alone cannot settle the turning question.

These are layout examples rather than surveyed installations. Bring photographs of normal parking to the appointment so the drawing reflects everyday use instead of an unusually tidy, empty driveway.

Wind exposure, privacy and the gate design

Discuss the amount of solid infill together with the location of the entrance. An exposed corner plot and a sheltered courtyard present different conditions. Give the installer information about strong gusts you have experienced, damage to earlier fittings and any planned removal of nearby screening. Ask how the proposed leaves, supports and operator suit that exposure.

Do not choose sliding solely because somebody calls it windproof, or fit a larger swing motor to compensate for unexplained resistance. The design needs to account for the complete assembly. A more open infill may deserve comparison where privacy requirements allow, but it still needs a site-specific assessment.

View the closed gate from inside and outside before committing to a privacy design. Consider visibility of visitors, headlights, the house frontage and any gap beside the stored sliding panel. Ask the drawing to show fencing or guarding required around the movement area, because those details also affect the finished appearance.

Plan walking access and breakdown arrangements

Decide whether pedestrians will use the vehicle entrance or a separate gate. Mark the intercom or keypad where a visitor can reach it without standing in the gate path. Show the route for a pushchair, wheelchair, bicycle and wheelie bin where relevant. A convenient vehicle opening can still leave an awkward daily walking route.

Ask the installer to explain access during a power cut or a mechanical fault before choosing the layout. Record who can operate the documented release, where instructions and keys will be kept, and how a released leaf will be controlled. A battery option should come with a defined supported configuration and maintenance arrangements.

For shared driveways, agree these arrangements with the people using the entrance. Discuss how work and future servicing can happen while residents still need access. Keep the access-control choice separate from the physical gate layout until both parts of the proposal have been checked together.

Compare installation and ownership costs

Ask both contractors to price an equivalent opening, finish and access-control brief. Separate gate fabrication, supports, operator equipment, power, excavation, drainage, protective measures and reinstatement. An inexpensive leaf can sit within a costly site project, while an existing suitable support or cable route may change the balance between proposals.

Record what each quotation excludes and which items remain allowances until inspection. Include waste removal, disruption to paving, access for installation equipment and any work by another trade. Ask who coordinates the finished levels if a driveway contractor is working at the same time.

Look beyond the initial total to the maintenance access, replacement-part support and finish care you are agreeing to. Request the service scope and written warranty terms for each proposal. There is no universal cost difference that makes one opening style the right choice for every London property.

Bring these details to a survey

Prepare photographs looking towards the gate and along both sides of the boundary. Add approximate opening dimensions, the usual parking arrangement and any planned change to the driveway. Identify drains, inspection covers and entrances that must remain accessible. Tell the surveyor whether you need a matching pedestrian gate, particular privacy or retained brick piers.

Ask for the recommended layout and at least one feasible alternative, with the reasons for rejecting any option that will not fit. Keep the resulting plan with the quotation so changes in panel size, supports or opening direction receive another check before manufacture.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a pair of gates need the entire opening width behind it?+
Each leaf has its own swept arc. Use the actual leaf dimensions and a site drawing that also accounts for vehicles, people and protective clearances.
Which is better for a short driveway?+
A sliding or folding design may help, but side space, supports, gradient and safe movement still need assessment.

Updated 2 October 2026

UK Electric Gate Safety: Responsibilities and Handover

Understand installer responsibilities, conformity documents and the difference between private-home and workplace gate maintenance duties.

On this page +
The completed entrance mattersInstaller and manufacturer responsibilitiesCE and UKCA marking in Great BritainPrivate homes, workplaces and landlordsTesting, maintenance and changesA practical handover checklistFAQs

The completed entrance matters

A powered gate is a machine. Its safety depends on the assembled gate, supports, drive, controls, protective measures and surroundings. A marked motor or a list of fitted sensors does not by itself demonstrate that the complete installation is safe.

A site assessment should consider the people who can encounter the gate, including visitors and children, and the places where movement could cause injury. The proposal and handover should explain how the identified risks are addressed.

Installer and manufacturer responsibilities

HSE explains that the person assembling a powered gate from components can become the manufacturer of the completed machine. Converting an existing manual gate to power operation can also create these responsibilities.

Ask who will take responsibility for the completed installation. Request the Declaration of Conformity, user instructions and the recommended maintenance and safety checks at handover. A component manual or motor receipt is not a substitute for the documents for the assembled gate.

CE and UKCA marking in Great Britain

Do not rely on the claim that CE marking stopped being accepted for gate equipment in January 2023. Current government guidance describes CE recognition alongside or in place of UKCA for relevant product regimes in Great Britain. The applicable rules depend on the product and market.

Ask the supplier to identify the conformity route and documents for the equipment and completed installation. See GOV.UK guidance on UKCA or CE marked products. Northern Ireland has separate arrangements.

Private homes, workplaces and landlords

HSE distinguishes private domestic owners from people responsible for gates at work or as part of a work activity. Its guidance says health and safety law does not apply to owners of gates on privately owned domestic premises, while recommending regular checks. This does not remove product or installer obligations, or a householder’s potential liability for harm or damage.

Commercial owners, employers, landlords and managing agents can have duties to keep gates safe. If your entrance serves rented property, a shared development or a business, establish who is responsible for its operation, maintenance and records. Do not use advice for a single private home as the complete answer for those settings.

Testing, maintenance and changes

The installer needs to assess and check the completed system before handover. Where force limitation forms part of the protection, its performance needs suitable verification. Read our force-testing explanation for what a homeowner should ask.

Follow the installation’s instructions and maintenance recommendations. Do not assume that one annual visit or a generic device list proves continuing safety. Report damage, unexpected movement or failed protective functions and seek competent help. Significant modifications may require a new conformity assessment; straightforward servicing is not automatically the same situation.

A practical handover checklist

Ask for the gate and equipment identification, operating instructions, manual-release training, isolation information, conformity documents and the recommended checking arrangements. Keep the responsible company’s contact details and agree what to do if a fault makes the entrance unsafe.

For an existing installation with missing records, request a gate assessment. Agree what the visit can establish rather than expect a certificate from photographs. Source: HSE guidance on responsibilities.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is UKCA the only acceptable marking for gate equipment in Great Britain?+
No blanket statement applies to every product. Current government guidance recognises CE alongside or in place of UKCA for relevant regimes. Ask the supplier to confirm the applicable route and documentation.
Must a private homeowner have an annual gate test by law?+

Winter Gate Maintenance for London Homes

Prepare your entrance for wet and cold weather with safe observations, the right service records and a clear fault plan.

On this page +
Check the entrance before colder weatherKeep homeowner care within the instructionsWhat to discuss at a service visitPrepare for a power cut or breakdownSeparate routine observations from repair workRain, leaves and underground equipmentFrost and changes in movementBook a service against an agreed scopePrepare the household for an interrupted entranceAfter a storm or an impact

Check the entrance before colder weather

From outside the movement area, look for damaged fittings, a leaning leaf, unusual gaps, standing water or debris near tracks and drains. Note changes in noise or movement during normal use. Do not repeat a faulty movement to investigate it.

Keep the gate instructions, service records and installer contact details together. Arrange an assessment before winter if the gate scrapes, hesitates or behaves differently. Tell the engineer about flooding, impact damage or recent paving work.

Keep homeowner care within the instructions

Carry out only the cleaning and care described for your installed system, using its stated isolation arrangements. Keep hands clear of hinges, rollers and trapping points. Do not remove electrical covers, change force settings or bypass sensors.

Lubricant type and application points depend on the equipment. Adding oil or grease to an unsuitable part can create problems. Ice, compacted debris and water in a motor enclosure need assessment; do not use force or improvised heat to restore operation.

What to discuss at a service visit

Ask the engineer to inspect the mechanical condition, supports, drainage, cabling and protective measures relevant to your entrance. Discuss how weather exposure and use affect the maintenance schedule. Request a record of findings, remedial work and checks before return to use.

Confirm the visit charge and what it covers before booking. Ask how parts or additional work will be authorised. A seasonal checklist cannot replace the maintenance instructions or an assessment of the complete system.

Prepare for a power cut or breakdown

Check that you have the correct user instructions and release key, and understand how the gate would be controlled and secured. Wind and gravity can move a released gate. Battery backup, where fitted, needs its own maintenance and capacity checks.

Read our manual-release guide before an emergency. If the motor hums without moving, stop repeated attempts and use our fault information checklist when requesting a repair assessment.

Further reading: HSE powered-gate safety and maintenance guidance.

Separate routine observations from repair work

SituationUseful homeowner informationWork to discuss with the engineer
A new scraping soundWhen it happens and whether the gate has changed position.Mechanical condition, alignment and the cause of contact.
Water after rainfallWhere water collects and when it disappears, observed from a safe place.Drainage, enclosures, connections and any affected equipment.
Intermittent openingWhich normal control was used and what response occurred.The relevant control route and complete gate behaviour.
Visible damagePhotographs from outside the movement area and known impact history.Stability, repairs and whether the gate should remain out of use.
Unknown service historyAvailable invoices, model details and handover documents.An initial assessment and a maintenance plan for the installation.

A checklist helps you describe changes; it is not permission to inspect moving parts. Keep observations brief and use what you have already noticed during normal use. If the gate is behaving dangerously, arrange help instead of collecting a better video of the fault.

Rain, leaves and underground equipment

Look at the whole entrance when discussing water problems. Tell the contractor about recent paving, blocked surface-water routes, new planting or a change in driveway levels. Photographs taken after rain can help explain where water gathers, provided you can take them without approaching exposed equipment or entering the movement area.

An underground operator may be out of sight, but its cover and maintenance access need to remain identifiable. Do not cover the area with planters, stored materials or a new surface without consulting the installer. Ask the engineer to check the drainage arrangement and explain what the owner may observe or clean under the supplied instructions.

Do not lift motor-box covers or bail water around electrical equipment as a general seasonal task. Report standing water and the symptoms you have seen. If the gate stops working after rain, tell the contractor whether other outdoor electrical equipment was affected, but leave electrical investigation to the appropriate competent person.

For leaves and debris, ask the installer to mark the areas the owner may safely maintain and the isolation steps that apply. A clear-looking track does not establish the condition of rollers, supports or equipment beneath a cover.

Frost and changes in movement

Report hesitation, unusual noise or a leaf that stops short instead of assuming cold weather explains it. Include the approximate weather conditions and whether the same behaviour occurred when the weather was milder. The engineer needs the actual model and condition to decide what to check.

Do not use boiling water, a blowtorch or another improvised heat source to free a gate. Avoid pulling on a powered leaf or repeatedly commanding it against ice or another obstruction. Follow the fault arrangements for the installation and keep people clear while access is restricted.

Ask for the specified care products and application points if the manufacturer permits owner lubrication. A general instruction to grease all hinges, tracks and racks ignores differences between systems. Keep the written instructions with the service record so a future owner does not inherit an unexplained bottle of lubricant and a guessed routine.

Book a service against an agreed scope

Give the contractor a list of changes since the previous visit. Mention building work, a vehicle striking the gate, replacement controls and any periods when the equipment was disconnected. Send the previous report so the engineer can see outstanding recommendations and parts already replaced.

Ask whether the quoted visit covers inspection only, routine servicing, adjustments, testing or fault diagnosis. Establish how additional work will be authorised and whether a further visit might be required for parts. Request the findings in writing rather than treating a service sticker as the complete record.

The maintenance interval should reflect the installed equipment and its use. A heavily used shared entrance and a lightly used private driveway need discussion on their own terms. Ask the contractor to explain its recommended interval and any circumstances that should prompt an earlier assessment.

Keep a simple owner log with the date, observed symptom, contractor contacted and outcome. Do not record guesses as confirmed diagnoses. For example, write that the gate stopped after heavy rain rather than declaring that the motor flooded unless the engineer has confirmed it.

Prepare the household for an interrupted entrance

Before poor weather arrives, check who has the instructions and knows whom to call. Keep the correct release key accessible to authorised users without storing it where visitors can misuse it. Ask for a demonstration at a service visit if you do not understand the documented procedure for your gate.

Discuss practical alternatives for arriving home, leaving for work and receiving deliveries while the gate is unavailable. A separate usable entrance can make a breakdown less disruptive. Do not rely on a courier or neighbour to improvise a release because they have used a different model before.

If backup power is fitted, ask what it supports, how its condition is checked and what happens when its capacity is exhausted. Record any warning indication the user should recognise. A working phone app does not establish that the motors have power or that the gate can move safely.

After a repair, ask what caused the problem, what changed and whether there is any revised owner care. Keep the new information beside the existing instructions. Seasonal preparation is most useful when it leaves the household with a clear access plan and a contractor with a reliable fault history.

After a storm or an impact

Check from a safe position whether the entrance looks different before returning to the usual routine. A fallen branch, leaning support or disturbed cable needs a report to the responsible contractor. Tell other household members about a restriction so somebody else does not operate the gate while you are arranging help.

Keep photographs and the timing of the event with the fault report. If another trade has been working nearby, share its description of the work with the gate engineer. Ask what must be repaired or checked before normal operation resumes, rather than assuming the absence of a visible obstruction resolves the problem.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should every gate be serviced once a year?+
Follow the system instructions and an engineer’s assessment of use, condition and exposure. A calendar interval alone does not establish that a gate is safe.
Can I increase the motor force in cold weather?+
Do not change safety or force settings to overcome a fault. Stop using a gate that struggles and arrange assessment.

How much do driveway gates cost in London?+

As a guide, fully installed electric sliding gates are typically £4,500 to £12,000 and electric swing gates £3,500 to £10,000. Do I need planning permission for driveway gates in London?+

Check the proposed height, position beside a highway, listed status, conservation-area controls, any Article 4 direction and planning conditions with the relevant authority. The rules depend on the property and work; opening inward alone does not establish permission.

How long does a driveway gate installation take?+

What type of gate is best for a London driveway?+

Can I automate my existing manual gates?+

Possibly, after assessment of the gate, supports, movement, surrounding hazards and proposed equipment. Ask what repairs or alterations are needed and compare the complete retrofit scope before buying motors.

Do you supply the gates as well as install them?+

We design, supply and install driveway gates and also discuss automation, repairs and maintenance. The written quotation will set out the agreed products, work, exclusions and handover arrangements.

Are electric gates safe for children and pets?+

A powered entrance needs a site-specific assessment, suitable protective measures and checks of the completed system. Children and pets must be considered in that assessment. A generic list of sensors does not by itself establish safety.

What happens if there is a power cut?+

Follow the user instructions for your installed system. Manual release and backup arrangements differ by product, and releasing a gate can allow uncontrolled movement. If you are unsure how to operate and secure it safely, keep clear and seek assistance.

Do driveway gates need planning permission?

Gates, fences and walls can usually be put up without planning permission under permitted development rights, as long as they are no more than 1 metre high where they are next to a road used by vehicles (or the pavement beside it), and no more than 2 metres high elsewhere. Height is measured from ground level. Because a driveway gate almost always faces the road, the 1 metre limit is the one that normally applies, so most full-height driveway gates need a planning application. The Planning Portal guidance on fences, gates and garden walls sets out the national rules.

Permitted development rights do not apply in the same way everywhere. Councils can remove them with an Article 4 direction, which many London boroughs use to protect front boundaries in conservation areas. Taking down an existing front wall or railings in a conservation area can need permission in its own right. Listed buildings need listed building consent for gates and boundary changes, and some newer homes have planning conditions that remove permitted development rights altogether.

Highway rules apply as well as planning. Gates must not open outwards over the pavement or road, so outward-opening gates need to be set back. A new or widened vehicle access needs the council’s approval for a dropped kerb, and trees covered by a tree preservation order can affect where posts and cables go.

If you are unsure whether your gates are permitted development, you can apply to the council for a lawful development certificate. On our survey we check the height, position and opening direction against these rules and tell you whether an application is likely to be needed. Planning decisions rest with your council, so always confirm the position for your own property using the borough resources above.

ANPR Gate Entry in London

ANPR (automatic number plate recognition) opens your gate or barrier by reading your car’s registration as you drive up. There’s no remote to find, no window to wind down and no keypad to reach. For households with several cars, staff car parks, residential developments and commercial yards, it’s the most convenient way to let regular vehicles in while keeping everyone else out. We supply and install ANPR entry for electric gates and barriers across London, integrated with intercoms and other access control.

How ANPR works

A dedicated ANPR camera watches the approach to the gate. It uses infrared light to read the reflective number plate clearly, day or night. Software reads the registration and checks it against a list of authorised vehicles. If it matches, the system sends an open signal to the gate’s control panel, exactly like pressing a remote. Unknown plates are ignored, logged, or passed to an intercom so the driver can call the house or reception.

This isn’t ordinary CCTV with software added. ANPR cameras use fast shutters and infrared lighting tuned to reading plates. A general security camera pointed at the drive will struggle, especially at night and with moving cars.

Camera position makes or breaks it

Most of an ANPR system’s reliability comes down to where the camera goes. It needs a clear view of the front plate as the car approaches, from a fairly shallow angle. It’s typically mounted on a post or wall at around bumper-to-roof height, 3 to 10 metres from where the car will be when the plate is read. Too steep an angle, a camera looking into low sun or headlights, or a bend in the approach all reduce read rates. We survey the approach, test the position and set up the camera on site with real vehicles before handover.

How reliable is it?

A well-installed system reads clean, standard UK plates very reliably. Reads fail on dirty or damaged plates, plates partly hidden by a towbar or bike rack, and illegal “show plates” with altered fonts or spacing. Foreign plates may also be missed. Motorbikes have no front plate, so they need another way in, or a camera placed to read the rear. That’s why every ANPR installation should keep a backup: a remote, keypad, GSM phone entry or intercom, so a missed read is a minor inconvenience, not a locked-out driver.

What it’s like to drive in

With a barrier, ANPR feels almost seamless. The barrier opens in a few seconds and most cars barely stop. With a swing or sliding gate, the gate still takes 15 to 25 seconds to open, so you’ll usually wait a short time unless the camera reads your plate well before you reach the gate. Placing the camera further down the approach helps where there’s room. Either way, the gate is designed to open fully before you drive through, and the car should never be waiting on the pavement or road. Exit is usually automatic, triggered by a sensor loop in the drive or an exit button, so you don’t need a second camera unless you want exit logs.

Managing vehicles

You manage the list of authorised plates through an app or web portal. Good systems make the everyday changes simple. You can add a new car, remove a sold one, or give a builder’s van access for the next three weeks only. Visitors expected on a particular day can be added with an expiry time, so their access stops automatically. Unknown vehicles can trigger the intercom or send a notification to your phone with a photo, so you can let them in with a tap. Many systems also tell you when a family member’s car has arrived home.

For residential developments and commercial sites, sort out early who has permission to add and remove plates, how residents or staff register a new car, and how quickly leavers are removed. A list that’s never reviewed gradually lets in people who should no longer have access.

Visitors and deliveries

ANPR handles vehicles you know about. For everyone else, pair it with an intercom placed where a visiting driver can reach it from the car window. Couriers and delivery drivers usually come in unknown vans, so a video intercom or GSM intercom that rings your phone is the practical answer. Our parcel delivery access guide covers this in more detail.

Local or cloud-based

Some ANPR systems do everything on the camera or a small unit on site, so they keep working if your internet goes down. Others use a cloud service for the plate list, the app and the logs, which makes remote management easy but adds a monthly subscription and depends on your connection. Many systems combine the two: plates are checked locally and synced from the cloud. We’ll explain which parts of the system you’re paying for monthly, and what still works if the subscription ends or the broadband fails.

Data protection

Number plates are personal data. On commercial sites and residential developments, the site operator is responsible for using ANPR lawfully under UK GDPR. That means signs telling drivers ANPR is in use, a clear reason for collecting the data, a set retention period for plate images and logs, and control over who can see them. For a private home, the ICO’s guidance is that data protection law applies if the camera captures images beyond your own property boundary, such as the public road. We aim cameras to cover your approach and as little of the street as possible, and set sensible retention periods by default. The ICO’s guidance on video surveillance sets out the full requirements.

Safety

ANPR decides whether a car is allowed to enter. It doesn’t decide whether the gate is safe to move. That’s still the job of the gate’s photocells, safety edges and force limits, tested to BS EN 12453. ANPR also doesn’t stop a second car following the first through an open gate, so on sites where tailgating matters, the gate or barrier should close promptly behind each vehicle.

Cost of ANPR gate entry in London

As a rough guide, adding ANPR to an existing electric gate at a home typically costs £1,500 to £3,500 installed, including the camera, set-up and integration. Commercial and multi-lane installations are usually £2,500 to £6,000 per lane. Cloud-managed systems usually carry an ongoing subscription, often somewhere between £10 and £50 a month depending on features and the number of vehicles. Every quote sets out the equipment, installation and ongoing costs separately.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will ANPR read every plate?+
It will read the vast majority of clean, standard UK plates when the camera is well positioned. Dirty, damaged, non-standard and foreign plates can fail, which is why a backup entry method is always included.
Can cars drive straight in without stopping?+
With a fast barrier, nearly. With a swing or sliding gate, expect a short wait while the gate opens, unless the camera can read the plate well before you reach it.
Does it work at night?+
Yes. ANPR cameras use infrared lighting and read plates in complete darkness.
What about motorbikes?+
Motorbikes only have a rear plate, so a front-facing camera won’t read them. Use a remote or keypad, or a camera positioned to read the rear plate.
What happens when I change my car?+
Remove the old registration and add the new one in the app. It takes seconds.
Does ANPR replace the gate’s safety devices?+
No. It only sends the open command. Photocells, safety edges and force testing are still required.

GSM Phone Entry for Gates in London

GSM phone entry lets you open your gate from any mobile phone, anywhere. There are no remotes to hand out and no broadband to rely on. The unit at the gate has its own SIM card and works over the mobile network. Family, carers, cleaners and regular visitors open the gate by calling a number. Visitors at the gate press a button and it rings your mobile, so you can let them in from the office, the school run or abroad. We supply and install GSM gate openers and intercoms, and add them to existing electric gates, across London.

Two kinds of GSM system

A GSM gate opener is a small unit wired into the gate’s control panel. You store a list of authorised phone numbers in it. When one of those numbers calls the unit, it recognises the caller ID, rejects the call and opens the gate. The call is never answered, so it normally costs the caller nothing. Calls from unknown numbers are ignored. It’s the simplest and cheapest way to give lots of people keyless access.

A GSM intercom adds a call panel at the gate for visitors. When someone presses the button, the unit rings your mobile (and then other numbers in turn if you don’t answer). You talk to the visitor and press a key on your phone to open the gate. Most GSM intercoms also work as an opener for authorised numbers. Video versions send a live picture to an app on your phone; see video intercoms.

Managing who can get in

Depending on the model, a GSM unit holds anywhere from a few hundred to several thousand phone numbers. Better units let you restrict numbers to set days and times (a cleaner on Tuesday mornings only), set numbers to expire on a date, and keep a log of who opened the gate and when. Most are managed by text message, a phone app or a web portal, so you can add or remove someone in seconds from wherever you are. When a carer or tenant leaves, you delete their number and their access stops immediately.

Some units can also tell you whether the gate actually opened. They do this by connecting to the gate’s position sensor and texting you a confirmation. That’s worth having if you open the gate remotely for deliveries and can’t see it.

The network switch-off

“GSM” originally meant the 2G mobile network, and many gate units still run on it. UK networks have now switched off 3G, and 2G will follow. The government’s agreement with the operators keeps 2G running until 2033 at the latest, but some services may wind down sooner. A unit bought today should be a 4G model, ideally one that supports voice calls over 4G (VoLTE), so it isn’t left stranded when older networks close. If you have an older 3G unit, it has almost certainly already stopped working. Ofcom’s switch-off guidance has the background.

SIM cards and running costs

The unit needs a SIM card that supports the services it uses: voice calls for opening and intercom calls, and texts for programming and alerts. Data is also needed for app-based models. A cheap SIM-only contract of a few pounds a month is the most reliable choice. Pay-as-you-go SIMs work, but many networks deactivate them if they’re not topped up or used for several months. A pay-as-you-go SIM in a gate that’s only opened by free rejected calls can quietly expire. Auto top-up avoids that. Intercom calls to your mobile come out of the gate SIM’s allowance, so busy entrances need a plan with enough minutes.

We record who owns the SIM and the admin account at handover. That way, if you move house or change installers, control of the system goes with the property and not with whoever set it up.

Signal, power and reliability

The unit only works as well as the mobile signal where it’s installed. Before installation, we test signal strength on the network you’ll use, in the exact position of the unit. A good signal on your own phone in the house is not the same test. Gate posts, metal enclosures and basement car parks can block reception. Where signal is weak, an external antenna on a short cable to a better spot usually solves it, or a different network can be used.

GSM entry doesn’t depend on home Wi-Fi or broadband, which is its big advantage over Wi-Fi gate systems. It does still need power. If the gate has battery backup, the GSM unit can usually run from it during a power cut. For the rare network outage, keep a remote or keypad as a backup way in. See keypad entry.

Security

GSM entry is as secure as the phones on its list. Keep the list up to date and remove numbers as soon as someone no longer needs access. Caller ID can in principle be faked, so for higher-security properties choose a unit that can require a PIN code during the call, or app control with proper log-in. Pairing GSM with a video intercom means you can see who you’re letting in rather than relying on a voice.

Where GSM works well

GSM entry suits homes with lots of regular visitors, holiday lets and Airbnb properties, where guest numbers can be added for the length of a stay. It’s also popular for elderly relatives with carers visiting at different times, shared driveways and small blocks of flats, and rural or outbuilding gates where broadband doesn’t reach. It works with any modern electric gate or barrier, including swing gates, sliding gates and car park barriers.

Cost of GSM phone entry in London

As a rough guide, a 4G GSM gate opener added to an existing electric gate typically costs £400 to £900 installed. An audio GSM intercom with a call panel is usually £900 to £1,800, and a 4G video intercom with app control £1,500 to £3,000. Add the SIM plan, usually a few pounds a month. Extra cabling, antennas and battery backup are itemised in the quote. Established makers such as AES, Videx and 2N all offer UK-supported 4G units.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will any SIM card work?+
Most standard SIMs from the main networks work, as long as the plan covers voice and text and suits the unit. Avoid data-only SIMs, and be careful with pay-as-you-go SIMs that expire if they’re not used.
Does it cost anything to open the gate?+
With a standard GSM opener, no. The unit rejects your call, so it isn’t answered or charged. Intercom calls from the gate to your mobile use the gate SIM’s minutes.
Do I need broadband or Wi-Fi?+
No. The unit uses the mobile network. It does need power, and a mobile signal at the gate.
Will the network switch-off affect my system?+
3G units have already stopped working. 2G units will stop working by 2033 at the latest. Any new unit should be 4G with voice over 4G (VoLTE) support.
How many people can I add?+
Usually hundreds and often thousands of numbers, depending on the model. Each one can be given time limits or removed individually.
Can I open the gate from abroad?+
Yes. If your phone can make a call or use the app, it can open the gate from anywhere.

Keypad Entry for Electric Gates in London

A keypad lets anyone with a code open your gate without carrying a remote. It’s usually the cheapest way to control who can get in through an automated gate. It suits homes where cleaners, dog walkers, family members and trades come and go at different times. You hand out a code rather than a fob, and if someone no longer needs access, you delete their code.

Wired or wireless

A wired keypad is connected by cable to your gate’s control panel and runs off the same power supply. It’s the most reliable option and needs no batteries. If the keypad sits on a post away from the pillar, though, a cable duct has to be laid under the driveway or verge. On a new installation that’s simple to plan in. On a finished block-paved drive it means lifting and relaying a strip of paving.

A wireless keypad runs on batteries and sends a coded radio signal to a receiver in the control panel. There’s no digging, so it’s the usual choice when you’re adding a keypad to a gate that’s already installed. Expect to change the batteries roughly every one to two years. On very thick brick pillars or long driveways the signal range needs testing on site first.

There’s also the question of where the codes are stored. A standalone keypad stores them itself and is programmed at the keypad. An app-managed keypad lets you add, delete and schedule codes from your phone, which is useful if you’re often away or let the property.

Codes, users and visitors

Basic keypads hold a handful of codes. Better models hold hundreds, each one separate, so you can remove the cleaner’s access without changing the code the family uses. Some also support time windows (a code that only works on Tuesday mornings, for example), codes that expire on a set date, and a log of which code was used and when.

When we hand the system over, we suggest six-digit codes rather than four. We also suggest a separate code for each regular visitor and a lockout after several wrong entries. We change the installer’s default master code in front of you, so nobody but you can reprogramme the keypad. Codes you give to people outside the household should be changed every so often. Worn buttons on a keypad that’s been used for years can show which numbers are in the code.

Where the keypad goes

For drivers, the keypad goes on a gooseneck post on the driver’s side, at roughly car-window height (about a metre). It’s set back far enough that the car waits clear of the gate while it opens. This matters most with outward-opening swing gates, where the post has to sit beyond the arc of the gate leaves. For people on foot, a keypad on the pillar beside a pedestrian gate at about chest height works well.

Many London front gardens are shallow. If there’s no room for a car to pull off the road before the gate, a driver using a keypad ends up waiting across the pavement. In that case a remote or ANPR for residents, with the keypad kept for visitors on foot, is often a better arrangement. If you’re in a conservation area, check our borough planning guides before adding a post to the front of the property.

Keypads facing the street need backlit keys for use after dark, a rain hood, and a rating of IP65 or higher for weather sealing. Where vandalism is a concern, look for an impact rating of IK08 or above.

Adding a keypad to an existing gate

Most gate control panels from the main brands (BFT, CAME, FAAC, Nice and others) have an input that a keypad can trigger, so adding one is usually straightforward. On the survey we check that the control panel has a spare input and enough power, we plan the cable or radio route, and we test the gate’s safety devices. A keypad is another way to start the gate moving. It does nothing to stop the gate hitting a person or a car. That’s the job of the photocells and safety edges required under BS EN 12453, and we won’t connect a keypad to a gate that isn’t safe to run automatically.

If the power goes off, a keypad on mains power stops working along with the gate, unless the system has battery backup. Make sure everyone who needs to get in knows how to release the gate manually, or has a key to the pedestrian gate.

Cost of keypad entry for electric gates in London

As a rough guide, a wireless keypad added to an existing automated gate typically costs £250 to £450 fitted. A wired keypad on a gooseneck post, including ducting and making good, usually comes to £500 to £1,000, depending on distance and the surface that has to be cut. App-managed keypads with scheduling and access logs sit at the upper end or above. We give a fixed written price after the survey.

Keypad, intercom or phone entry?

A keypad suits people you trust to let themselves in. If you want to see and speak to visitors before opening the gate, look at video intercoms. If you’d rather open the gate from your mobile wherever you are, GSM phone entry does that, and many homes combine it with a keypad. For couriers specifically, see our parcel delivery access guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I give a delivery driver or tradesperson a temporary code?+
Yes, with a keypad that supports timed or expiring codes. You set the code to work for a set period and it stops working after that. Basic standalone keypads can’t do this, so tell us at survey stage if you need it.
How many codes can a keypad hold?+
It depends on the model. Entry-level keypads hold a few codes, while mid-range and app-managed units hold hundreds, each separate from the others.
What if someone finds out a code?+
Delete that code or change it. You don’t need to change anyone else’s, as long as each person has their own code. A lockout after repeated wrong entries stops anyone trying codes until one works.
Does the keypad work in a power cut?+
Only if the gate has battery backup. Otherwise use the manual release or the pedestrian gate key until power is restored.
Can you fit a keypad to a gate someone else installed?+
Usually, yes. We check the control panel, the power supply and the gate’s safety devices on the survey first.

Video Intercoms for Gates in London

A video intercom lets you see who’s at the gate, talk to them and let them in, from a screen in the house or from your phone wherever you are. It’s the standard way to handle visitors and deliveries at a gated home. You don’t have to walk down the drive, and you never have to open the gate to someone you haven’t seen. We supply, install and integrate video intercoms with new and existing electric gates across London, alongside keypads, GSM phone entry and ANPR.

How it works

A visitor presses the call button on a panel at the gate. The panel has a camera, microphone and speaker. The call rings on one or more screens inside the house and, on most modern systems, on your phone through an app. You see and speak to the visitor, then press a button to open the driveway gate, the pedestrian gate or both. The intercom simply tells the gate’s control panel to open, just like a remote. The gate’s own safety devices still control how it moves.

Types of system

Two-wire systems send video, audio and power along a single pair of cables. They’re robust and reliable over long distances, often more than 100 metres, which suits long drives. They’re also ideal where an old intercom cable already runs from the gate to the house and can be reused. Comelit, Videx and Fermax all make well-regarded two-wire ranges. Many now add app calling through a gateway unit.

IP systems run over network cable, usually a single external-grade Cat6 cable carrying data and power (Power over Ethernet) up to about 100 metres. They give the sharpest video, app calling, multiple monitors, recording and easy integration with CCTV, and are increasingly the default for new installations. Hikvision, Akuvox, 2N and DoorBird are common choices.

Wireless and Wi-Fi systems avoid digging a cable trench, but a gate is often 20 to 50 metres from the house, sometimes behind brick walls and metal gates. Home Wi-Fi rarely reaches reliably. Where trenching isn’t practical, a point-to-point wireless link (a pair of small dishes) is far more dependable than Wi-Fi. For gates with no cable route at all, a 4G video intercom works over the mobile network instead. See GSM phone entry.

Getting the signal to the house

Most of the work in a video intercom installation is the cable route. The cable runs in a duct, usually under the drive or along a boundary, from the gate to the point where it enters the house. If you’re having the drive relaid or new gates installed, put the duct in then. It costs far less than lifting paving later. We survey the route, check any existing cables and agree where the indoor monitor and network connection will go before quoting.

The gate panel

Choose an external panel built for life outdoors on a street. It should be weatherproof (IP65 or better) and vandal-resistant, with a wide-angle camera, infrared night vision so you can see faces after dark, and wide dynamic range so a visitor isn’t just a silhouette against bright sky or headlights. Panels can include a keypad or fob reader, so the same unit handles visitors and residents.

Mount the panel at around 1.4 to 1.5 metres for people on foot. For drivers, fit a second panel on a gooseneck post at car-window height, or mount it where the driver can reach it without leaving the car or stopping across the pavement. On commercial sites, a third panel at lorry-cab height is common. See car park barriers.

Inside the house

Indoor monitors range from simple 4 or 7-inch screens to 10-inch touchscreens that can also show CCTV cameras. You can have several, such as one in the kitchen, one upstairs and one in a home office, and they can all ring together or in sequence. Monitors can also act as an internal intercom between rooms.

Answering on your phone

App calling forwards the call to your phone, so you can let in a delivery driver or cleaner while you’re out. It relies on the gate panel having a network connection and your phone getting the notification. Expect a few seconds’ delay compared with an indoor monitor, and make sure the system will still ring the indoor monitor if your broadband goes down. Some apps need a subscription for remote access or cloud recordings. We’ll tell you exactly what’s included before you buy.

Linking to the gate

The intercom connects to the gate’s control panel to open the gate. It can also connect to a second relay for an electric lock on a pedestrian gate. Most modern gate control panels from the main manufacturers accept an intercom without difficulty. Older or unusual ones sometimes need an interface or an upgrade, which we check at survey. If you want the intercom to show whether the gate is actually open or closed, that needs a gate position sensor wired back to the intercom, and not every system supports it.

Recording and privacy

Many systems save a snapshot or short video clip each time someone calls, either on a memory card in the monitor, on a recorder or in the cloud. That’s useful for checking deliveries and visitors you missed. If the camera captures images beyond your property, such as the street or a neighbour’s house, data protection law applies even at home. The ICO’s guidance on domestic CCTV explains your responsibilities. We angle cameras to cover the visitor, not the pavement opposite, and many panels let you mask out areas you don’t want recorded.

Rough costs of video intercom systems in London

As a rough guide, a two-wire video intercom with one indoor monitor, connected to an existing gate, typically costs £900 to £2,000 installed. IP systems with app calling and multiple monitors usually cost £1,500 to £3,500. Premium panels with integrated keypads, fob readers and high-end cameras run £2,500 to £5,000. Trenching, ducting and reinstating the drive are itemised separately, and any app or cloud subscriptions are shown in the quote. Our intercom buying guide and Comelit vs Hikvision comparison go into the brands in more detail.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a video intercom work with my existing gate?+
Almost always, with modern gate control panels. Older or unusual control panels sometimes need an interface. We check the make and model at survey.
Can I answer the gate from my phone?+
Yes, with an IP system or a two-wire system with an app gateway. You’ll need broadband at the house (or a 4G intercom), and some apps charge a subscription.
Do I need a cable from the gate to the house?+
For the most reliable system, yes, run in a duct. Where that’s not possible, a point-to-point wireless link or a 4G intercom are good alternatives. Home Wi-Fi usually isn’t reliable enough.
Can I reuse my old intercom cable?+
Often, with a two-wire system designed for exactly that. We test the existing cable first.
Does it record visitors?+
Many systems save a snapshot or clip for every call. Continuous recording usually needs a CCTV recorder. Check which you’re getting before you buy.
Can it open a pedestrian gate too?+
Yes. Most intercoms have two outputs, one for the driveway gate and one for a pedestrian gate lock.

Aluminium gates for your London home

Choose the appearance of the entrance first: open bars, horizontal slats or a boarded design that provides more screening. Then compare the construction behind that appearance. Profile dimensions, joints, support posts and hardware matter as much as the colour.

Bring photographs of your frontage and examples of the look you prefer to the initial discussion. We can consider the driveway layout with you before specifying a gate. An existing pillar or a narrow entrance may need changes that a product photograph cannot show.

Choose the opening before ordering the gate

A swing gate needs a clear movement area inside the entrance. A sliding system needs suitable space along the boundary and a support arrangement designed for that system. The survey should account for gradients, drainage, parking positions and a separate route for people on foot.

Look at electric sliding gates and electric swing gates to compare the layouts. Avoid ordering from the width of the opening alone: the installer also needs to check supports, clearances and exposure.

Finishes, colours and samples

Ask for a sample and the exact colour reference for the proposed finish. Confirm whether the same colour applies to both faces, posts, hinges and other visible hardware. Wood-effect and textured finishes have their own product specifications and availability.

Check the manufacturer’s instructions for cleaning and dealing with scratches. Aluminium still needs appropriate care, and a powder-coated finish does not carry one universal guarantee.
