Composite Driveway Gates in London

Composite gives you the look of a boarded timber gate without the sanding, staining and painting. The boards don’t rot, splinter or need recoating, and they hold their colour far better than untreated wood. We design, supply and install composite driveway gates on aluminium frames for homes across London, as manual gates or automated swing and sliding gates.

Get a Free QuoteCall 020 3773 1310
Free Site SurveysWritten Fixed Quotes
MaterialsFramesDesignCompareAutomationCarePlanningCostFAQsGet a quote

What composite actually is

Most composite gate boards are wood-plastic composite: a blend of wood fibre and recycled plastic, extruded into boards with a wood-grain texture. They’re stable, rot-proof and need no paint. Not all composite boards are equal, and the biggest difference is whether the board is capped.

Capped (co-extruded) boards have a tough polymer shell bonded around the core. That shell resists fading, staining, scratches and mould far better, and keeps the colour close to the sample you chose. This is what we recommend for gates.

Uncapped boards are cheaper first-generation products. They lighten noticeably in their first months outdoors, absorb more moisture and are more prone to marks and mould. They’re common in budget fence panels, and are the main reason some people think composite looks tired after a few years.

Colours range from greys and charcoals to warm browns and teaks. Dark boards look striking, but they get hot in direct summer sun and show dust more, which is worth bearing in mind on a south-facing frontage.

Frames and construction

Composite boards aren’t strong enough to form a gate on their own, so they’re fitted into a powder-coated aluminium frame. The boards slot into channels in the frame, so there are no visible screws on the face, and a damaged board can be slid out and replaced rather than the whole gate being rebuilt. Aluminium won’t rust, keeps the gate’s weight down, and comes in colours to match or contrast with the boards. Anthracite and black frames are the most popular.

Composite expands and contracts with temperature more than timber does, mostly along the length of each board. A properly designed gate leaves room for that movement in the frame channels. Boards screwed tight into a homemade frame can bow or buckle in a hot summer.

Privacy, design and wind

Most composite gates are horizontal boarded. Boards set tight together give full privacy, while small gaps between them let light and air through and give you a glimpse of the road as you pull out. Gates can be flat-topped, which is the most common and suits modern houses, or finished with an aluminium slatted top section. A matching pedestrian gate and composite fence panels keep the whole frontage consistent.

A solid boarded gate catches the wind like a sail. That doesn’t rule it out, but on exposed or wide entrances the frame, hinges, posts and any motors need to be sized for wind load as well as weight. Leaving small gaps between boards noticeably reduces the load.

Composite, timber or aluminium?

Compared with timber, composite needs no staining or painting, won’t rot or split, and keeps a consistent colour. Real wood looks and feels more natural up close, can be planed and refinished, and is often preferred in conservation areas. See wooden driveway gates.

Compared with aluminium, composite has a softer, more wood-like texture and a warmer look. All-aluminium slatted gates (including wood-effect finishes) are lighter, slimmer and offer more design options, especially for very wide or sliding gates. See aluminium driveway gates.

Automation

Composite gates on aluminium frames automate well. Swing gates take ram, articulated arm or underground motors, chosen to suit the gate’s width, weight and wind exposure, the depth of your piers and how the gates need to open. Where the drive slopes up behind the gate, or there isn’t room for leaves to swing, a composite sliding gate is often the better answer. See electric swing gates, electric sliding gates and our swing vs sliding guide. If you already have a gate you’d like to motorise, see gate automation retrofits.

Looking after a composite gate

Composite is low-maintenance, not no-maintenance. Wash the boards with warm soapy water and a soft brush once or twice a year, more often near busy roads where traffic grime builds up. A pressure washer is fine on a low setting held well back from the surface. Capped boards can’t be sanded, so deep scratches are dealt with by replacing the board. Grease the hinges and check the fixings once a year, and have any motors and safety devices serviced to the installer’s schedule. Composite manufacturers typically offer long warranties on capped boards, often 10 years or more, so keep the paperwork.

Planning permission

Under permitted development rules, gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high without planning permission. Taller gates need consent, and conservation areas and listed buildings have stricter rules. Composite can be a harder sell in some conservation areas than timber or traditional metal. Our borough planning guides cover the local position.

Cost of composite driveway gates in London

As a rough guide, a pair of aluminium-framed composite driveway gates typically costs £2,500 to £5,000 supplied and fitted, depending on width, height and board specification. Automation usually adds £2,500 to £6,000. Sliding gates, new posts, pier work, groundworks and matching fence panels are quoted separately. Our gate cost guide has a checklist for comparing quotes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do composite gates need maintenance?+
Very little. A wash once or twice a year, plus annual hinge greasing, keeps them looking right. They never need painting or staining. Automated gates also need regular servicing of the motors and safety devices.
Will composite fade?+
Capped boards fade very little, though all outdoor materials soften slightly in colour over time. Uncapped boards lighten much more noticeably, which is why we recommend capped boards for gates.
Can a composite gate be automated?+
Yes. On an aluminium frame it’s lighter than most hardwood gates. The motor has to be matched to the gate’s size and wind exposure, especially for solid boarded designs.
How much do composite gates cost?+
Typically £2,500 to £5,000 for a manual pair supplied and fitted, with automation on top. We give a fixed itemised price after a free survey.
Can a damaged board be replaced?+
Yes. On a slot-in frame, a single board can be removed and replaced without taking the gate apart. That’s one reason to choose a proper gate system rather than fence boards fixed to a frame.

Electric Sliding Gates in London

Sliding gates suit London homes where swing gates struggle: short front drives, cars parked close to the gate, and drives that rise behind the entrance. The gate moves sideways along the inside of your boundary, so it never sweeps into the drive or out over the pavement. We design, supply and install electric sliding gates in aluminium, steel, timber and composite, from compact single gates on terraced houses to wide entrances on detached homes.

Why choose a sliding gate?

A pair of swing gates on a 3.5-metre opening needs roughly 2 metres of clear drive behind it for the leaves to open. On many London frontages, that space is where the car parks. A sliding gate needs almost no depth. You can park right up to it and it still opens. Sliding gates also cope with drives that slope up from the road. The gate travels across the entrance rather than swinging into the slope, so what matters is the ground along the gate line, not the gradient of the drive. They’re also less affected by wind than a pair of long swing leaves, and generally more secure, because there’s no centre joint to force.

The trade-off is side space. The gate needs somewhere to go when it’s open.

Tracked, cantilever or telescopic

Tracked gates run on wheels along a steel rail across the entrance. They need side space roughly equal to the opening plus a few hundred millimetres for the motor and end post. For a 3.5-metre opening, allow about 4 metres of straight, clear fence line or wall. They’re the most economical sliding gate and suit most London homes. The track has to be kept clear of leaves and grit, and needs drainage so water doesn’t pool against it. They’re a poor fit for gravel drives, because stones get into the track.

Cantilever gates hang from rollers fixed to a foundation beside the opening, so nothing touches the ground across the entrance. They give a clean threshold that works with gravel, block paving or resin, and there’s no track to clean or freeze. In return, they need more side space, because the gate carries a counterbalancing tail, typically adding 40 to 50 percent to the gate’s length. A 3.5-metre opening needs around 5 metres of run. Our heavy-duty sliding gates page covers larger cantilever gates for commercial sites.

Telescopic gates are made of two or more panels that slide over each other, so the open gate takes up roughly half the side space. They’re the answer when your boundary turns a corner or meets the house close to the entrance. They need a little more depth, because the panels sit side by side when open, and they cost more than a single-panel gate.

Checking the side space

The run-back area is the strip behind your fence or wall where the open gate sits. It needs to be straight, roughly level along its length, and clear of obstructions. Common problems on London properties are downpipes and gas meters on the side of the house, steps and doorways, trees and roots, inspection chambers and a neighbour’s fence that isn’t straight. We measure all of this at survey and give you a drawing showing the clear opening, where the gate sits when open, and the foundations.

Safety in the run-back area

A sliding gate can trap someone in two places: at the closing edge, where it meets the end post, and in the run-back area, where a person or child could be caught between the moving gate and a wall or fence. We fit photocells across the opening and safety edges on the gate’s leading and trailing edges. Where the gate runs close to a fence, wall or open area, the run-back is guarded with mesh or a fixed panel so nobody can get between them. Closing forces are tested and recorded against BS EN 12453 at handover. You’ll also be shown how to release the gate by hand. See our manual release guide.

Motors and features

Residential sliding gates use a motor mounted on a plinth inside the boundary, driving a toothed rack fixed along the gate. 24V motors are the usual recommendation for homes. They slow the gate gently at each end, detect obstructions precisely and can run on battery backup in a power cut. Light aluminium gates can use a nylon rack, while heavier steel and timber gates need a galvanised steel rack.

A typical domestic sliding gate opens at around 15 to 25 centimetres per second, so a 4-metre gate takes roughly 20 seconds to open fully. A part-open setting for people on foot is worth having. It opens the gate about a metre so you can walk through without waiting for the full opening. Sliding gates work with every type of access control: video intercoms, keypads, GSM phone entry and ANPR.

Gate material and finish

Aluminium is the most popular material for sliding gates. It’s light, so it’s easy on the motor and rollers, it doesn’t rust, and it comes in slatted, solid and wood-effect designs. See aluminium driveway gates. Steel suits traditional bar designs and should be galvanised and powder-coated. Timber and composite sliding gates are built on a steel or aluminium frame to keep them rigid. Fully solid gates catch the wind, so they need a correctly sized motor and well-fixed guide rollers. A matching pedestrian gate completes the frontage.

Installation

Tracked gates need a concrete strip across the opening for the track, and a plinth for the motor. Cantilever gates need a reinforced foundation along the run-back to carry the rollers. We lay ducting for power and control cables at the same time, and cut and reinstate paving or tarmac around the work. Tracked gates are usually installed in two to three days. Cantilever gates are installed in two visits about a week apart, so the foundation can cure before the gate is hung. If you’re resurfacing the drive, tell us early. It’s much cheaper to put foundations and ducts in before the new surface goes down.

Cost of electric sliding gates in London

As a rough guide, a tracked electric sliding gate for a typical 3.5 to 4-metre residential opening costs £5,000 to £9,000 supplied and fitted with motor and basic controls. Cantilever gates usually cost £7,000 to £12,000, and telescopic gates £8,000 to £13,000. Automating an existing sliding gate is typically £2,000 to £3,500. Intercoms, extensive groundworks and drive reinstatement are itemised separately. See our installed gate cost guide for more.

Looking after a sliding gate

Have the gate serviced once a year. A service covers checking the motor, rack, rollers and safety devices, testing the closing force and testing the battery backup. In between, keep the track clear of leaves and stones, keep the photocell lenses clean, and don’t let plants grow into the run-back area. See gate repair and servicing if the gate starts sticking or reversing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much side space does a sliding gate need?+
For a tracked gate, roughly the width of the opening plus a few hundred millimetres. For a cantilever gate, about one and a half times the opening. A telescopic gate needs about half the opening plus the overlap. We measure it precisely at survey.
Can a sliding gate work on a sloping drive?+
Usually, yes. A drive that slopes up from the road is often the reason people choose a sliding gate. What needs to be level is the ground along the gate line and the run-back, not the drive itself. A gate sliding along a slope needs a stepped or raked design and careful engineering.
Swing or sliding?+
Sliding if your drive is short, you park close to the gate, or the drive rises behind it. Swing if you lack side space or want the lower cost. Our swing vs sliding guide compares them, and electric swing gates covers the alternative.
Will a tracked gate work on a gravel drive?+
Not well, because stones get into the track and jam the wheels. A cantilever gate is the better choice on gravel.
How long will installation take?+
Two to three days for most tracked gates. Cantilever gates take two visits about a week apart. Larger groundworks or new power supplies add time.
Do I need planning permission?+
Gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high under permitted development rules. Taller gates, conservation areas and listed buildings need checking. See our borough planning guides.

Telescopic Sliding Gates in London

A telescopic sliding gate is made of two or more panels that slide over each other as the gate opens, a bit like a telescope closing. When it’s open, the panels sit stacked beside the entrance, taking up roughly half the side space of an ordinary sliding gate. On London plots where the boundary meets the house, turns a corner or runs into a neighbour’s wall close to the entrance, that’s often the difference between a sliding gate fitting or not. We design, supply and install telescopic sliding gates for homes and commercial sites across London.

How a telescopic gate works

A standard sliding gate is one panel. It needs side space at least as wide as the opening, because the whole panel has to slide clear. A telescopic gate splits that panel into two (or sometimes three) narrower panels on parallel tracks.

The motor drives the front panel, which travels the full width of the opening. A cable, belt or pulley system links it to the rear panel, which moves at half the speed and travels half the distance. Both panels start and finish together, arriving neatly side by side behind the end post when open and overlapping slightly in the middle when closed. Everything runs from one motor and one set of controls, just like a single sliding gate.

How much space you need

Side space. A two-panel gate needs roughly half the opening, plus an overlap of a few hundred millimetres. A 4-metre opening, which would need about 4.3 metres of side space with a standard tracked gate, needs only around 2.3 metres with a two-panel telescopic gate. A three-panel gate needs about a third of the opening plus overlaps, so around 1.6 metres for the same 4-metre opening. The survey gives exact figures for your entrance.

Depth. Because the panels sit side by side when open, a telescopic gate needs more depth behind the boundary than a single gate. Allow roughly 300 to 450 mm for a two-panel gate, depending on the gate thickness and running gear. Most front drives have that easily, but it’s worth checking where a path or flower bed runs along the inside of the boundary.

A level, clear run. As with any sliding gate, the ground along the gate line and the parking area for the open panels needs to be straight and roughly level, and clear of downpipes, meters, steps and tree roots.

When telescopic is the right choice

Telescopic gates make sense when a sliding gate is the right idea but a single panel won’t fit. Typical London examples include:

  • the house wall, garage or a side passage gate meeting the boundary just beyond the entrance
  • a corner plot where the boundary turns
  • a mature tree or protected hedge beside the opening
  • a wide double-width drive where there’s room for half the gate on one side but not the whole of it

They also work well where swing gates would clash with parked cars or a drive that rises behind the gate. Those are the same reasons people choose sliding gates in the first place. See electric sliding gates for the wider picture.

Tracked or cantilever

Most residential telescopic gates are tracked, with each panel running on its own steel rail across the entrance. That makes them reliable and economical, but both tracks need to be kept clear of leaves and grit, and they’re not well suited to gravel drives.

Cantilever telescopic gates have no tracks across the opening. They’re less common, more complex and more expensive, and they still need a counterbalancing tail, so they save less space. We generally recommend them only where a clean threshold is essential and the side space allows.

The trade-offs

A telescopic gate has more moving parts than a single panel: two sets of wheels, two tracks and the linking mechanism. That means a higher price, a little more maintenance, and a mechanism that needs correct tensioning to keep the panels in step. Two panels side by side are also slightly more visible from inside the property than a single gate.

There’s also an extra safety point. Where the panels pass each other, there’s a shearing point that has to be guarded. We fit safety edges and cover any gaps so fingers can’t be caught between the panels, alongside the usual photocells and safety edges on the leading edge. Closing forces are tested and recorded against BS EN 12453 at handover.

Materials

Aluminium is the best material for telescopic gates. Keeping the panels light reduces the load on the motor, wheels and linking mechanism, and aluminium won’t rust. It suits slatted, solid and wood-effect designs. See aluminium driveway gates. Galvanised steel works for heavier-duty and commercial gates. Timber and composite infill can be used on an aluminium or steel frame, but heavy solid panels are generally better avoided on telescopic gates. Remember that solid panels catch the wind, and a telescopic gate has two of them.

Motors and controls

Telescopic gates use the same motors as standard sliding gates. 24V motors are the usual choice for homes, because they slow the gate gently at each end, detect obstructions precisely and can run on battery backup in a power cut. A part-open setting lets the gate open about a metre for people on foot. Every type of access control works with them: video intercoms, keypads, GSM phone entry and ANPR.

Installation

Each track sits on a concrete foundation across the opening, alongside a plinth for the motor and an end post where the panels close. Ducting for power and controls goes in at the same time, and the paving or tarmac is made good around the work. Most residential telescopic gates are installed in two to four days, depending on the groundworks.

Cost of telescopic sliding gates in London

As a rough guide, a two-panel aluminium telescopic sliding gate for a typical 3.5 to 4.5-metre residential opening costs £8,000 to £14,000 supplied and fitted with motor and basic controls. Three-panel gates, steel construction, cantilever designs and wider commercial openings cost more. Intercoms and extensive groundworks are itemised separately. See our installed gate cost guide.

Looking after a telescopic gate

Have the gate serviced once a year. A service covers the motor, safety devices and closing force test, plus the tension of the linking mechanism and the condition of the wheels and rollers on both panels. In between, keep both tracks clear and the photocell lenses clean. If the panels start arriving out of step, the linking mechanism probably needs adjusting. See gate repair and servicing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much side space does a telescopic gate need?+
For a two-panel gate, roughly half the opening plus a few hundred millimetres. For three panels, about a third of the opening plus the overlaps. The survey gives exact figures.
Are telescopic gates reliable?+
Yes, when they’re well built and serviced. The extra wheels and the linking mechanism need a little more attention than a single-panel gate, which is why an annual service matters.
Telescopic sliding gate or bi-folding gate?+
Both save space. A telescopic gate needs side space but almost no depth. A bi-folding gate folds back into the drive, so it needs depth but no side space. Which works better depends on where your spare room is.
Can I convert my existing sliding gate to telescopic?+
Rarely. The panels, tracks and running gear are designed as a system, so it’s normally a new gate. The motor and access control can sometimes be reused.
Do I need planning permission?+
The same rules apply as for any gate. Usually up to 1 metre high next to a road or footpath without permission, with stricter rules in conservation areas and for listed buildings. See our borough planning guides.

How much space do you need?

A swing gate needs clear space for each leaf to open fully, plus a margin. For a typical 3.5-metre opening with a pair of gates, each leaf is about 1.75 metres long. That means a clear arc of roughly 2 metres behind the gate line, with no parked car, bin, step or planter in the way. Your car also has to stop outside the arc while the gates open, or wait on the road if it can’t. On a short London front drive, that is often what decides between swing and sliding.

A pair of gates halves the arc each leaf needs, so it’s the usual choice on driveways. A single leaf works well for narrower openings up to about 3 metres, or where one side of the drive is blocked by a wall, tree or step. For a comfortable entrance from a narrow road, aim for an opening of at least 3.5 to 4 metres. Turning in from a tight street with parked cars opposite needs more width than driving straight in.

If space behind the gate is tight, a sliding gate or bi-folding swing gate may be the better answer. Our swing vs sliding guide compares the layouts.

Sloping driveways

A drive that rises behind the gate is the most common problem with swing gates, because the bottom of the leaf hits the ground partway through its swing. There are a few ways round it. The gate can be made with a raked or stepped bottom rail that follows the slope. It can be hung higher, leaving a larger gap under it when closed. It can open outwards, if that’s permitted (see below). Or you can switch to a sliding gate. Fitting a more powerful motor doesn’t solve a slope problem. A drive that falls away behind the gate is much less of an issue. Our guide to automated gates on sloping driveways goes into more detail.

Can the gates open outwards?

Not over a public pavement or road. Section 153 of the Highways Act 1980 lets the council require any gate that opens outward onto a highway to be altered, and a gate swinging into pedestrians or traffic is a real hazard. Outward opening is only an option where there’s private land, such as a private drive or a deep verge you own, between the gate and the pavement. Our outward-opening gate guide explains the rules, and your borough’s planning guide covers gate height and conservation area limits.

Choosing the motor

Ram motors are mounted on the inside face of the gate and pier. They’re the most common and most economical option, suit most residential gates, and are easy to service. They need a modest amount of space between the hinge and the inside edge of the pier, which most London piers have.

Articulated arm motors have a folding arm, like a door closer. They suit deep brick piers where the hinge is set well back from the inside face and a ram won’t fit. They can also open gates past 90 degrees.

Underground motors sit in a steel box buried under each hinge, so nothing is visible above ground. They’re the choice for period homes, ornamental ironwork and anyone who wants a completely clean look. They cost more to install, and the foundation boxes must drain properly, usually to a soakaway or drain, because a flooded box will eventually kill the motor.

There’s also the question of power. 24V low-voltage motors are now the standard recommendation for homes. They slow down gently at each end of the travel, sense obstructions precisely, and can run on battery backup during a power cut. Mains-powered (230V) motors and hydraulic motors are tougher for very heavy gates and high-use entrances. We use established brands such as BFT, CAME, FAAC and Nice, chosen to suit the gate’s weight, length and wind exposure.

Safety

Every automated gate has to be safe for the people around it, including children, visitors and delivery drivers who’ve never seen it before. We fit photocells across the opening and, where needed, safety edges on the leading edge of each leaf. We check the gap at the hinge side where fingers could be trapped, and the space between the open leaf and any wall, where someone could be crushed. Closing forces are tested and recorded against BS EN 12453 at handover. Then we show you how to release the gates by hand. Our manual release guide covers the common systems.

Wind and locking

Solid boarded gates catch the wind like a sail, which strains the motors and can push the gates open. Long leaves, solid infill and exposed sites benefit from a central ground stop for the leaves to close against, and an electric lock that holds them shut. Both reduce the load on the motors and improve security.

Power and cabling

Your gates need a dedicated electrical supply, run from your consumer unit to the control panel by the gate, with an isolator switch nearby. The cable between the two leaves runs in a duct under the drive. If you’re having the drive relaid, put the ducting in at the same time and save digging later. Access control, such as an intercom, keypad, GSM phone entry or ANPR, is planned with the cabling.

Cost of electric swing gates in London

As a rough guide, automating an existing pair of swing gates with ram motors typically costs £2,500 to £4,500 installed. Articulated arm motors are similar to slightly more. Underground motors usually run £4,000 to £7,000. A complete installation with new gates, motors and access control generally costs £5,000 to £12,000 or more, depending on the gate material and design. Groundworks, new piers and intercoms are itemised separately. See our installed gate cost guide for more.

Automating existing gates typically takes one to two days. Underground motors and new gate installations take longer because of the groundworks.

Looking after electric swing gates

Have the gates serviced once a year. A service covers checking the motors and safety devices, testing the closing force, adjusting the travel limits, greasing the hinges and testing the battery backup. Between services, keep the photocell lenses clean and the area behind the gates clear. See gate repair and servicing if anything starts behaving oddly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should swing gates open inward?+
Almost always, if the gate is on the boundary with a public pavement or road. Outward opening is only possible over private land, and the arc still needs to be kept clear of anywhere people walk.
What width should I choose?+
At least 3 metres for a car, and 3.5 to 4 metres if you’re turning in from a narrow street. Make sure there’s space behind the gates for the leaves to open with your car parked beyond them.
Are swing gates cheaper than sliding gates?+
Usually, because they need less groundwork. But a swing gate on a slope or tight drive can need costly workarounds, and then a sliding gate can cost about the same.
Can you automate my existing gates?+
Often, yes, if the gates are rigid, the hinges are sound and the piers are strong enough. See gate automation retrofits.
What happens in a power cut?+
24V systems can run on battery backup for a number of cycles. Otherwise, each leaf can be released with a key and opened by hand.
How long do the gates take to open?+
Typically 15 to 25 seconds, depending on leaf length and motor type.

Can your gates be automated?

Many manual gates can be automated, but not every one. A motor moves the gate; it doesn’t fix it. If a gate drags on the ground, sags at the closing end or sticks when you push it by hand, a motor will strain against it and fail early. We fix that first or tell you plainly that replacement is the better option.

On the survey we check that each leaf is straight and moves freely by hand, that the hinges are sound, and that the posts or pillars can take the extra load. Brick pillars that are cracked or loose often need reinforcing or replacing with steel posts. We also weigh up the gate’s width, weight and design: solid boarded gates catch the wind and need a stronger motor than open railings.

The ground matters too. Swing gates need room to open without hitting the drive or the car, and gates must not swing out over a pavement or road. Sliding gates need a level run beside the opening. If your gates have dropped over time, our guide to sagging driveway gates explains the usual repairs.

Choosing the right motor

For swing gates there are three main types. Articulated-arm motors fit on the face of the pillar and suit deep pillars and gates hung close to them. Linear rams need space behind the pillar but give smooth, controlled movement. Underground motors sit in a box beneath each hinge and are almost invisible, which suits period and high-end entrances, but they need good drainage.

Sliding gates use a ground-mounted motor that drives a toothed rack along the gate. We match the motor to the gate’s weight and width and to how often it will be used, rather than fitting a one-size kit. Low-voltage 24V motors can run on battery backup for a limited number of cycles in a power cut. Read more about underground gate motors.

Power, cabling and groundwork

Automated gates need a dedicated fused supply from your consumer unit, run in armoured cable to the control panel by the gate. For swing gates, a cable also has to cross the entrance to reach the second motor, usually in a duct under the driveway. On a finished block-paved or resin drive that means cutting a narrow channel and making good afterwards, and we include that in the quote.

A new outdoor circuit is notifiable electrical work under Part P of the Building Regulations, so it must be carried out or certified by a registered electrician. Where running mains power is impractical, a solar-powered system can work for lighter, less frequently used gates.

Safety comes first

Powered gates can cause serious injury, so automation is about more than the motor. Every installation we fit is set up with the photocells and safety edges the gate needs under BS EN 12453, and the closing force is measured and recorded. Our force testing guide explains what that involves.

At handover we show you how to release the gates manually in a power cut and give you the test records. We won’t leave a gate running automatically if it isn’t safe to do so.

Ways to open the gate

Most people start with handheld remotes and add other controls as needed. A keypad lets family, cleaners and trades in with their own codes. A video intercom lets you see and speak to visitors first, GSM phone entry opens the gate from your mobile, and ANPR opens it automatically for registered cars. Common faults and what usually causes them

The gate won’t move at all

Start with the power. A tripped breaker or RCD at the consumer unit, or a fused spur switched off near the gate, accounts for a surprising number of call-outs. If the power is fine, the cause is often water in the control panel, a failed control board, or a cable damaged by digging, roots or rodents.

The gate opens but won’t close, or reverses halfway

This is almost always the safety photocells. They’re the pair of small sensors either side of the opening, and if anything breaks the beam between them, the gate won’t close. Dirt on the lenses, a plant growing across the beam, or a sensor knocked out of line will stop the gate closing. Low winter sun shining straight into a receiver can do the same at certain times of day.

Only one leaf moves

On a pair of swing gates this points to a fault on that motor. The usual suspects are a failed capacitor, a stripped gearbox or a broken wire. It can also be the manual release on that leaf, left unlocked after someone opened the gate by hand.

Grinding, clunking or juddering

Worn gearbox teeth, a seized hinge, or a sliding gate’s rack and pinion out of alignment. On sliding gates, stones or leaves in the track and worn guide rollers cause the same symptoms. Keep using a noisy gate and a small repair can turn into a motor replacement, so take it out of automatic use until it’s looked at.

The gate has dropped or catches on the ground

Hinges and posts move over time, especially with heavy timber gates and on clay soil. Once a leaf drags, the motor works harder and wears faster. Rehanging or adjusting the gate often fixes this without touching the automation.

Remotes or the keypad don’t work, but the gate runs from other controls

Check the remote’s battery first. If that isn’t it, the receiver may have lost its stored codes or failed. Re-coding or replacing a receiver is a short job.

Checks you can do before calling us

Make sure the power is on at the consumer unit and at any isolator switch near the gate. Try a second remote or the keypad to rule out a flat battery. Wipe the photocell lenses and check nothing is blocking the beam. On a sliding gate, clear the track. If you’ve used the manual release recently, check it’s been locked again, because the gate won’t run on its motor while it’s released.

If the gate moves erratically, makes a new noise, or has hit something, stop using it on automatic and keep people and cars clear of it. Our manual release guide explains how the common systems are released by hand. Don’t force a leaf that won’t release easily, and don’t open the control panel.

What a service includes

A proper service is more than greasing the hinges. We test every safety device: photocells, safety edges and the obstacle detection that makes the gate stop and reverse when it meets resistance. We measure closing force against the limits in BS EN 12453. We check hinges, posts, motor mountings and, on sliding gates, the track, rollers and rack. Limits and run times are adjusted, battery backup is tested if fitted, and all remotes, keypads and intercoms are checked. You get a written report that separates three things: what we fixed, any safety concerns, and optional improvements. That way you can see what genuinely needs doing.

For a typical home gate, once or twice a year is sensible. Busier entrances, such as shared driveways, blocks of flats and commercial sites, usually need servicing every quarter. Keep the service records. Many manufacturer warranties depend on regular servicing, and the records help any engineer diagnose faults later. Commercial owners have legal duties to keep powered gates safe, explained in the HSE powered gate safety guidance.

Older and unsafe gates

Some older installations were fitted without photocells or with obstacle detection set far too high. We can repair the reported fault on these gates. If the gate isn’t safe to run automatically, though, we’ll tell you so and quote for the upgrade it needs. In most cases, adding safety devices to an existing gate is a modest cost compared with replacing it.

Cost of electric gate repairs and servicing in London

As a rough guide in London, a diagnostic visit is typically £95 to £150, often credited against the repair if you go ahead. A routine service usually costs £120 to £250, depending on the gate and how many access controls it has. Common repairs vary widely. Replacing a pair of photocells is usually a few hundred pounds fitted. A new control board or a replacement motor costs more, depending on the brand. We give you an itemised price before any work beyond the agreed diagnosis goes ahead.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can you repair a gate another company installed?+
Yes. Gates from the mainstream manufacturers are straightforward to work on. Unbranded or discontinued systems can be harder to get parts for. In that case we’ll tell you which parts can still be repaired and which need replacing.
How quickly can you come out?+
We prioritise gates that are stuck open or trapping a car in or out. Tell us when you call if that’s your situation.
How long does a repair take?+
Most faults are fixed in a single visit of one to three hours. If a specific part has to be ordered, the gate can usually be left safely in manual mode while you wait, typically a few working days.
My gate is making a grinding noise. Should I keep using it?+
No. Stop using it on automatic and book a repair. Grinding usually means worn gears or a misaligned drive, and running it on tends to turn a part replacement into a new motor.
What warranty do repairs carry?+
New parts carry the manufacturer’s warranty and our workmanship is guaranteed in writing. Parts of the system we haven’t replaced aren’t covered by that guarantee, and the report will say which those are.

Oak, iroko and sapele are dense, naturally durable and heavy enough to feel genuinely solid when you close them. With proper joinery they last for decades. We make and install hardwood driveway gates for period homes, country-style properties and contemporary houses across London, as manual gates or automated.

The main hardwoods for gates

European oak is the traditional choice and the most asked for on period homes. It’s strong, naturally durable and has the classic straight grain with silvery flecks. For gates we use kiln-dried oak, not green (freshly sawn) oak. Green oak is cheaper but shrinks and twists as it dries, which is fine for a rustic barn but not for a pair of gates that need to meet neatly in the middle. Oak is rich in tannins, which react with ordinary steel and leave black stains, so all fixings and ironmongery should be stainless steel or galvanised. Tannins also wash out in the first few months and can mark pale paving below the gate. Rinsing the gate down a few times after installation helps.

Iroko is often called “poor man’s teak”. It’s naturally oily, very durable and more stable than oak, so it’s less prone to movement and surface cracking. It starts a golden yellow-brown and darkens to a deep brown. It’s usually cheaper than oak and suits both traditional and contemporary designs, including horizontal slatted gates.

Sapele has the reddish-brown colour and fine grain of mahogany. It’s stable, machines cleanly and takes a finish beautifully, which makes it a good choice for formal, highly finished gates. It’s a little less durable than iroko, so it relies more on a well-maintained finish.

Idigbo and meranti are budget hardwoods. Idigbo is pale and reasonably durable, but stains with iron like oak does. Meranti quality varies a lot from batch to batch. Both are a step up from softwood, though we’d usually point anyone spending real money towards oak, iroko or Accoya.

Accoya often comes up in the same conversation. Strictly, it’s not a hardwood. It’s a modified pine that is more stable and durable than most hardwoods and ideal for painted gates. See our Accoya guide and the main wooden driveway gates page.

Where the timber comes from

Every hardwood we use comes with FSC or PEFC certification, which shows it was grown and harvested responsibly. Under the UK Timber Regulations, suppliers must also show the timber was legally harvested. This matters most with tropical hardwoods like iroko and sapele. If a quote is suspiciously cheap, ask where the timber came from.

How hardwood gates are built

Hardwood’s weight is both its strength and its challenge. A solid oak driveway leaf can easily weigh 120 kg or more. Unless the gate is built to carry that weight, it will sag at the latch end within a few years.

A properly made hardwood gate has a frame joined with mortise and tenon joints, glued and secured with hardwood pegs. Diagonal braces run upwards from the bottom hinge towards the latch side, carrying the weight back to the hinges. Stiles (the vertical frame members) are often laminated, built up from bonded layers so they resist twisting, which matters most on gates that will be automated. Infill boards are tongue-and-groove or properly spaced, so they can move with the seasons without splitting the frame. On very wide or heavy gates, a hidden galvanised steel frame inside the timber takes the structural load entirely.

Posts, hinges and fittings

Heavy gates need heavy supports. Hardwood posts should be substantial (typically 200 to 250 mm square for driveway gates), set deep in concrete, and ideally kept off direct ground contact with a steel post shoe so the base doesn’t rot. On brick piers, hinges are fixed into sound brickwork with resin anchors. Old piers often need repairs or rebuilding before they’ll carry a hardwood gate, and we check that at survey.

Use adjustable, bolt-through hinges, so the gate can be realigned if it settles. On a drive that rises behind the gate, rising butt hinges or careful hinge positioning lift the leaf as it opens so it clears the slope. Alternatively, a sliding gate avoids the problem entirely.

Manual gates need the right fittings to be practical day to day. That means a drop bolt into a ground socket to hold one leaf shut, a central stop for the leaves to close against, ground-mounted holders or hooks to keep the gates open in the wind, and a good lock or padbolt. Getting these right is the difference between a gate you’re happy to use and one you leave open because it’s a nuisance.

Finishes

Hardwood gives you a genuine choice. A hardwood oil or UV-filtered translucent stain keeps the warm colour and shows the grain. On an exposed south-facing gate, expect to re-coat every year or two. Sheltered gates go longer. The surface just needs cleaning and a fresh coat, not stripping. Iroko’s natural oils can stop some coatings bonding properly, so use a product designed for oily hardwoods.

Leaving the gate unfinished lets oak and iroko weather naturally to a soft silver-grey. This is the lowest-maintenance option, because the timber’s natural durability protects it. Just accept some surface checking (fine cracks) and a change of colour within the first year or two.

Paint is possible on hardwood but rarely the best use of it. If you want a painted gate, Accoya generally holds paint longer and costs less than painted oak. Accoya publishes care guidance for its own timber. For hardwoods, follow the coating manufacturer’s instructions.

Whatever finish you choose, it should be applied in the workshop to every surface, end grain included, before the gate is hung.

Automating hardwood gates

Hardwood gates automate well, but they need more from the motor than lighter gates. The motor must be sized for the leaf’s weight and the wind load on a solid boarded gate, not just its width. Hydraulic and heavy-duty electromechanical rams and underground motors all handle hardwood comfortably when correctly specified. Motor brackets should be through-bolted with backing plates, because screws alone eventually pull out of the timber. An electric lock helps hold heavy leaves closed against wind. See electric swing gates. To motorise an existing hardwood gate, see our retrofit automation service. We’ll check that the frame, hinges and posts are up to it first.

Planning permission

Gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high under permitted development rules. Taller gates need planning permission, and conservation areas and listed buildings have stricter controls. Hardwood gates are often well received by conservation officers on period properties. See our borough planning guides.

Cost of hardwood driveway gates in London

As a rough guide, a pair of iroko or sapele driveway gates typically costs £3,000 to £6,500 supplied and fitted, and oak usually £4,000 to £8,000, depending on width, height and design. Large or highly detailed bespoke gates can be £8,000 to £12,000 or more. Automating heavy hardwood gates usually adds £3,000 to £7,000. New posts, pier repairs and old-gate removal are quoted separately. Our cost guide explains how to compare quotes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long will a hardwood gate last?+
A well-built oak or iroko gate commonly lasts 30 years or more. The joinery, how well the end grain is sealed and how the gate is hung matter as much as the species. Cheap hardwood gates with screwed joints fail far sooner.
Oak or iroko?+
Oak for a traditional look on a period property and the classic silvered finish if left unfinished. Iroko for better stability, a warmer colour and usually a lower price. We bring samples of both to the survey.
Can hardwood gates be automated?+
Yes, with motors sized for their weight and wind load, and a frame rigid enough not to sag. Through-bolted brackets and an electric lock are good practice on heavy leaves.
Will I need to stain the gates every year?+
Only if you want to keep the original colour, and even then exposed gates typically need re-coating every one to two years, sheltered ones less often. If you’re happy for the timber to turn silver, it needs no staining at all.
Why has my new oak gate left dark marks on the paving?+
That’s tannin washing out of fresh oak. It eases off after the first few months. Rinsing the gate and paving a few times early on, and using stainless fixings, keeps it to a minimum.
Wood or aluminium?+

What metal gates are actually made of

Almost every “wrought iron” gate sold today is made from mild steel. True wrought iron hasn’t been produced commercially for decades and only survives in reclaimed and antique work. Mild steel is strong, easy to shape into scrolls and bars, and can be welded and repaired. Its weakness is rust, so the finish matters more than anything else.

Aluminium is far lighter than steel and doesn’t rust, which makes it a natural fit for wide gates, sliding gates and automation. It’s usually powder-coated and suits contemporary slatted and panel designs particularly well. Decorative aluminium castings let it imitate traditional styles too. See aluminium driveway gates for more.

Some modern gates also use stainless steel for a bright architectural look, or weathering steel (often sold as Corten), which develops a stable rust-coloured surface by design.

How the finish protects the gate

This is where cheap metal gates and good ones differ most. The gold standard for steel is hot-dip galvanising followed by powder coating, often called a duplex finish. The finished gate is dipped in molten zinc, which coats it inside and out, including the welds and the insides of hollow bars where rust usually starts. A powder coat is then baked on top for colour. A duplex-finished gate commonly lasts 25 years or more before it needs any serious attention.

Powder coat applied straight onto bare steel looks identical on the day of installation. Once it chips, though, water gets underneath and rust creeps along the steel under the coating, typically showing first at welds and the bottom rail within a few years. Wet-painted steel is cheaper still and needs repainting regularly. When comparing quotes, ask exactly which of these you’re getting, and whether galvanising is done after all the welding.

Colour is personal, but black remains the classic for traditional gates and anthracite grey (RAL 7016) has become the default for contemporary ones. Satin and textured finishes hide fingerprints and marks better than gloss. Our colour trends article has examples.

Choosing a design

Traditional designs include straight-top, arched and swan-neck (concave) gates, with vertical bars finished in spear, ball or fleur-de-lis tops and details such as collars and scrolls. These suit period houses and are often what conservation areas expect. Bow-top gates give a softer, rounded look.

Contemporary designs lean on horizontal slats or flat bars, solid or perforated sheet panels, and laser-cut patterns. The gap between slats decides how much privacy you get and how much of the road you can see as you pull out. Our slat gate guide goes into spacing and sightlines. For full privacy with a softer look, a steel frame with timber or composite infill combines the strength of metal with the warmth of wood.

If you have children or a dog, keep gaps between bars and under the gate below 100 mm so they can’t squeeze through or get stuck. Horizontal rails on the outside face make a gate easy to climb, so on security-conscious frontages they’re best kept on the inside.

Posts, hinges and weight

A pair of steel driveway gates can weigh several hundred kilograms, so they need solid supports. Steel box-section posts concreted into the ground are the most reliable option. Existing brick piers can be used if they’re sound, with hinges fixed into the brickwork with resin anchors. Adjustable hinges (or ball-bearing hinges on heavier gates) let the leaves be realigned if anything settles over time. Aluminium gates put much less load on posts and piers, which can make them a better choice where the existing brickwork is weak.

Automation

Metal gates automate very well. The best results come when automation is planned before fabrication: motor brackets and fixing points are welded on before the gate is galvanised, so nothing needs drilling or welding afterwards that breaks the protective coating. Steel swing gates suit ram, articulated arm or underground motors. Where space is tight, a metal gate can be built as a sliding gate instead. See electric swing gates, electric sliding gates and our swing vs sliding guide.

Restoring old metal gates

Original Victorian and Edwardian gates are often worth saving, especially on listed buildings and in conservation areas, where the planners may expect them to stay. Restoration usually means removing the gates, blast-cleaning back to bare metal, repairing or recasting damaged sections, then refinishing. Steel can be galvanised. Cast iron is usually primed with a zinc-rich primer instead, because the heat of galvanising can crack it. Our restoration article and wrought iron gates page cover this in more detail.

Planning permission

Under permitted development, gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high without planning permission. Taller gates need consent, and conservation areas, listed buildings and Article 4 directions (which remove some permitted development rights) add further restrictions. See our borough planning guides.

Looking after a metal gate

A galvanised and powder-coated gate needs very little care. Wash it down with water and mild detergent once or twice a year, particularly near main roads where traffic grime builds up. Touch up any chips with a zinc-rich primer and matching topcoat before rust can start. Grease the hinges and check the fixings annually. If it’s automated, have the motors and safety devices serviced too.

Cost of metal driveway gates in London

As a rough guide, a pair of made-to-measure galvanised and powder-coated steel driveway gates typically costs £2,500 to £6,000 supplied and fitted, depending on width and design. Highly ornate or fully bespoke work can be £6,000 to £12,000 or more. Aluminium gates are generally similar to slightly higher for the same design. Automation usually adds £2,500 to £6,000. New posts, pier repairs and groundworks are quoted separately. Our gate cost guide has more detail.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are all metal gates galvanised?+
No, and many cheaper gates aren’t. Ask whether the gate is hot-dip galvanised after fabrication, then powder-coated. That combination is what keeps rust away for decades.
Is a “wrought iron” gate really wrought iron?+
Almost certainly not, unless it’s antique. Modern iron-style gates are mild steel, which is just as good-looking and easier to repair.
Steel or aluminium?+
Steel is stronger, heavier and better for intricate traditional ironwork. Aluminium is lighter, can’t rust, and is better for wide gates, weak piers and sliding gates. Both can be made in traditional or modern styles.
Can you restore an existing iron gate?+
Usually, yes. We check whether it’s steel, wrought iron or cast iron and how much corrosion there is, then advise whether restoration or replacement makes more sense.
Are metal gates maintenance-free?+
Not quite, but close if they’re galvanised and powder-coated. An occasional wash, touching up chips and greasing the hinges once a year is usually all they need.

Pedestrian and Side Gates in London

A separate pedestrian gate means you don’t have to open the driveway gates every time someone walks in. Visitors, postmen and children on foot get their own way in, and the big gates stay shut. A good side gate is also one of the most effective security improvements you can make, because the side passage is the most common way burglars reach the back of a house. We design, supply and install front pedestrian gates, side passage gates and matching sets for homes and shared entrances across London.

How wide should it be?

Think about everything that needs to pass through, not just people. Most front pedestrian gates are 900 mm to 1 metre wide. For wheelchair access, aim for at least 850 mm of clear opening once the gate is hung. That’s measured between the open gate and the opposite post, not the width of the gate itself, because the hinges, the stop and the thickness of the open leaf all take space. Double buggies need about the same.

Side passage gates have extra traffic. A standard wheelie bin is around 600 mm wide, but you’ll want room to wheel it without scraping your knuckles, and to get bikes, lawnmowers and building materials through. If the passage allows, 1 metre or more makes everyday life easier. Communal bins on blocks of flats are much wider and usually need a double gate.

Securing a side passage

Police crime-prevention advice on side gates is consistent. Fit the gate as close to the front of the house as possible, so there’s no hidden recess for someone to work in. Make it at least 1.8 metres tall, with no horizontal rails or cross-braces on the outside to climb. Lock it from the inside. Hinges should have pins that can’t be knocked out, or be fixed with security screws. A solid boarded timber or steel-framed gate with a top rail at the same height as the fences either side is far harder to get over than a low gate with a trellis top. Our driveway and home security guide covers the rest of the frontage.

Locks, latches and closers

For a side gate, a key-operated lock with a thumb-turn on the inside is the most practical setup. You can lock it from the garden without a key and open it from the street with one. Add heavy-duty bolts top and bottom on the inside for extra security when you’re away.

For a front pedestrian gate, a gate lock with handles on both sides lets you open it normally and lock it at night. Traditional timber gates often use a Suffolk latch or ring latch for a period look.

A hydraulic gate closer brings the gate shut automatically and stops it slamming. That’s useful if you have children or a dog, or if visitors and delivery drivers never shut gates behind them. Closers have to be matched to the gate’s weight and paired with a latch that catches reliably as the gate closes. A closer fighting a stiff latch leaves the gate open. Self-closing hinges are a simpler, cheaper option for light gates.

Electric locks and entry systems

A pedestrian gate can be fitted with an electric lock and opened by an intercom, keypad, fob reader or GSM phone entry. That’s how most homes let visitors in without walking down to the gate.

There are two main types of electric lock, and the difference matters if the power fails. A magnetic lock holds the gate shut only while it’s powered, so it releases in a power cut. That’s the safe choice on any gate that people may need to leave through in an emergency, such as the entrance to a block of flats. An electric strike or solenoid lock stays locked when the power goes, which is more secure but must always have a manual way to open it from the inside. From inside, people leave by a handle, a push-to-exit button or both. On shared entrances and escape routes, the arrangement must allow everyone out quickly in a fire, so it needs to be agreed with whoever manages the building.

Electric locks need a cable to the gate, usually in a duct under the path. Planning it at the same time as the driveway gate automation saves digging twice. See access control systems.

Separate gate or wicket door?

A separate pedestrian gate has its own opening beside the driveway gates. It’s the better option if there’s room. It gives a level walking route, works independently of the vehicle gates, and lets people walk in without stepping into the path of a moving gate.

A wicket is a small door built into one leaf of a larger gate. It’s useful where there’s no space for a separate opening, and is common on large timber gates and commercial entrances. The drawbacks are a raised threshold (often a step-over bottom rail, which is awkward for buggies and wheelchairs unless a low-threshold design is used) and a narrower opening. On a powered gate, a wicket needs a safety switch so the main gate can’t move while the wicket is open. It’s an important safeguard that cheaper installations sometimes leave out.

Materials and matching

Pedestrian gates are made in every material we use for driveway gates: timber and hardwood, steel and wrought iron style, aluminium and composite. If you’re also having driveway gates made, ordering the pedestrian gate at the same time keeps the colour, board pattern, bar spacing and finials identical. Matching an existing gate later is possible, but a perfect match is harder, especially with weathered timber or older ironwork.

Fitting

Side gates in London are often hung between a house wall and a neighbour’s fence or wall. They can be fixed with hinge plates into sound brickwork, or with a steel or timber post where the masonry won’t take the load. The gate should open inwards, away from the street. Where the ground rises behind the gate, the gate has to be set high enough to clear the slope, or hung on rising hinges. A small gap under the gate and attention to drainage stop water pooling or the bottom rail rotting.

Planning permission

Under permitted development rules, gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high without planning permission. Gates elsewhere, such as a side gate set back from the pavement, can usually be up to 2 metres. Conservation areas, listed buildings and Article 4 directions (which remove some permitted development rights) can restrict this further. See our borough planning guides.

Cost of pedestrian and side gates in London

As a rough guide, a timber side gate typically costs £350 to £900 supplied and fitted. A steel or aluminium side gate is usually £600 to £1,500. A pedestrian gate made to match new driveway gates generally adds £800 to £2,000 to the project, depending on material and design. Adding an electric lock with a keypad or intercom typically costs £800 to £2,500, depending on the system and cable route. Our gate quotation checklist helps when comparing quotes for the whole entrance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can the pedestrian gate match my driveway gates?+
Yes. Made at the same time, it can match the material, colour, infill pattern and details exactly. Matching an older gate is usually possible too, though weathered timber and historic ironwork can take more work.
What width should a pedestrian gate be?+
Usually 900 mm to 1 metre for a front path gate, with at least 850 mm of clear opening if wheelchair users need access. Side passage gates benefit from 1 metre or more for bins and bikes.
Can I use an intercom or keypad with a side gate?+
Yes, with an electric lock. Choose a lock type that suits what should happen in a power cut, and make sure there’s always an easy way to open the gate from inside.
How tall should a side gate be for security?+
At least 1.8 metres, with no climbable rails on the outside, and fitted as close to the front of the house as possible.
Should I choose a separate gate or a wicket in the driveway gate?+
A separate gate if there’s room. It gives a level, independent walking route. A wicket is a good fallback where space is tight, but expect a threshold to step over and a narrower opening.

Wooden Driveway Gates in London

Timber is still the most popular choice for driveway gates on period houses across London, and for good reason. It suits Victorian and Edwardian brick, it’s often what conservation officers want to see, and a solid boarded gate gives more privacy than almost any metal design. We design, supply and install wooden driveway gates in softwood, hardwood and Accoya, as manual gates or fully automated.

Which timber?

Treated softwood (usually redwood or pine) is the budget option. It’s pressure-treated against rot, takes paint well and keeps costs down. It’s also less stable than hardwood, so it’s more likely to twist or shrink, and it needs regular repainting to last. With good care, expect something like 10 to 15 years.

European oak is the traditional choice for period and country-style gates. It’s very strong, heavy and naturally durable, and left unfinished it weathers to a soft silver-grey. Oak contains tannins that react with ordinary steel, causing black staining around fixings and on pale paving in the first year or two. Proper oak gates use stainless steel or galvanised fittings for that reason. Oak also moves and develops small surface cracks (known as checks) as it dries, which is normal.

Iroko and other tropical hardwoods such as sapele give a rich golden-brown colour, high natural durability and better stability than oak, often at a lower price. Ask for FSC or PEFC certification, which shows the timber comes from responsibly managed forests.

Western red cedar is light, stable and naturally rot-resistant, with a warm reddish tone. Its lightness makes it easy to automate, but it’s soft and dents more easily than hardwood.

Accoya is sustainably grown pine that’s been chemically modified so it barely absorbs water. It’s one of the most stable and durable timbers available. It holds paint for much longer than ordinary wood, and the manufacturer offers a long warranty on the timber itself. It costs more than most hardwoods, but suits painted gates that you want to stay straight and crisp for decades. Our Accoya guide explains how the timber warranty differs from a warranty on the finished gate.

How a good wooden gate is built

Most cheap wooden gates fail at the joints, or through sagging. A well-made gate has a frame joined with mortise and tenon joints, glued and pegged, not screwed or nailed. Diagonal braces run upwards from the bottom hinge to the top of the latch side, so they carry the weight back to the hinges. Fitted the wrong way round, they do nothing. The boarding is tongue-and-groove or properly spaced, so the timber can swell and shrink with the seasons without splitting or bowing.

Large gates, and any gate that’s going to be automated, benefit from laminated stiles (the vertical frame members), which are made from several bonded layers and resist twisting. Very large or heavy gates can be built around a hidden galvanised steel frame clad in timber, so the leaves never sag however wide they are.

Design options

Solid boarded gates with a flat, arched or swan-neck top are the classic choice for period homes and give full privacy. Gates with an open top section of spindles or a fretwork panel let you see the road as you leave and look less imposing from the street. Horizontal slatted designs, often in iroko, cedar or Accoya, suit contemporary houses. Hardware matters too. Black forged hinges and ring handles look right on a traditional gate, while concealed hinges and slim stainless fittings suit a modern one.

Finish and upkeep

You have three realistic choices. Paint (a microporous system that lets the timber breathe) gives a crisp colour and good protection, and needs recoating every few years depending on timber and exposure. Accoya extends that interval considerably. A translucent oil or stain shows the grain and is easy to refresh, but needs reapplying more often, typically every year or two on south-facing gates. Leaving hardwood unfinished to silver naturally is the lowest-maintenance option, as long as you’re happy with the grey colour and some surface checking.

Whatever finish you choose, it should be applied in the workshop to every face of the gate, including the end grain and the edges that won’t be visible once the gate is hung. The end grain soaks up water like a straw if it’s left bare, and that’s where rot starts. A quick wash down each spring and a check of the finish on the bottom rail, which takes the worst of the rain splash, will add years to any wooden gate.

Automating a wooden gate

Timber gates automate well, with a few conditions. Solid hardwood is heavy, and a solid oak leaf can easily weigh more than 100 kg. A solid boarded gate also catches the wind, so the motor has to be sized for both the weight and the wind load, not the weight alone. The gate needs a rigid frame that won’t sag or twist. Otherwise it will drift out of alignment with the motor and the closing stop.

For period homes, underground motors are popular because they’re hidden in the ground beneath the hinge and leave the gate looking traditional. Ram motors mounted on the inside face are the most common and economical choice. Articulated arm motors suit deep brick piers where a ram won’t fit. See electric swing gates for how these compare. If you already have a wooden gate you’d like to motorise, see gate automation retrofits. We’ll check the gate is sound enough first.

Posts and piers

Hanging a heavy wooden gate on undersized posts or crumbling brick is the quickest way to make it sag. Timber posts should be substantial hardwood, typically 200 mm square or more for driveway gates, set deep in concrete. On brick piers, hinges are fixed with resin anchors into sound brickwork. Some old piers need rebuilding or reinforcing before they can carry a new gate, and we check that at survey rather than discovering it on installation day.

Planning permission

Under permitted development rules, gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high without planning permission. Anything taller needs consent. Conservation areas, listed buildings and properties with Article 4 directions (which remove some permitted development rights) have stricter rules. Our borough planning guides cover the local position. In many conservation areas, a well-designed timber gate gets a smoother reception than metal.

Cost of wooden driveway gates in London

As a rough guide, a pair of treated softwood driveway gates typically costs £1,200 to £2,500 supplied and fitted. Hardwood such as iroko or oak usually runs from £3,000 to £7,000 for a pair, depending on size and design, and Accoya sits at or slightly above that. Automation typically adds £2,500 to £6,000, depending on motor type, with underground motors at the top of that range. New posts, rebuilt piers and groundworks are quoted separately. Our gate cost guide has more detail.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long do wooden gates last?+
It depends mostly on the timber and how well it’s looked after. Treated softwood typically lasts 10 to 15 years with regular painting. Good hardwood and Accoya gates commonly last 25 years or more. Joinery quality and how well the end grain is sealed matter as much as the species.
Can wooden gates be automated?+
Yes, if the gate is rigid and the motor is sized for its weight and wind load. Heavy solid gates and wide leaves need more powerful motors, and gates with a weak frame should be rebuilt before they’re automated.
Which timber should I choose?+
For a painted gate you want to stay straight with minimal fuss, choose Accoya. For a traditional natural look on a period property, oak or iroko. For a lighter contemporary slatted gate, cedar or iroko. On a tight budget, treated softwood is the sensible choice. We bring samples to the survey so you can see each one against your house.
Will my wooden gate warp?+
All timber moves a little with the seasons, so boards may show small gaps in summer and tighten in winter. Proper joinery, stable timbers and laminated stiles keep that movement from becoming warping or sagging.
Wood or aluminium?+
Aluminium is lighter, needs almost no maintenance and is available in convincing wood-effect finishes. Real timber looks and feels better on many period homes. Our wooden and aluminium comparison covers the trade-offs, and our hardwood gates page goes deeper on oak and iroko.

Wrought Iron Gates in London

Ornamental ironwork defines London’s period streets. Victorian squares, Edwardian villas and Georgian terraces all relied on railings and gates with spear tops, scrolls and collars. We make new traditional iron-style gates and railings, and restore original ironwork, for homes across London. That covers matching a pattern that’s been on the street for 150 years, or designing something new in the same spirit.

Wrought iron, cast iron or steel?

The name “wrought iron gate” usually describes a style, not the metal. Knowing what’s in front of you matters, especially if you’re deciding whether to restore or replace.

True wrought iron was hand-worked by blacksmiths and is no longer produced commercially. It has a fibrous grain, almost like wood, and when it corrodes it tends to flake apart in layers. Original gates show forge-welded or riveted joints and hand-tapered scroll ends. If you have genuine wrought iron, it’s almost always worth saving.

Cast iron was poured into moulds and used for the crisp, repeated ornament on Victorian railings: finials, rosettes, panels and decorative posts. It’s hard and resists corrosion well, but it’s brittle. It cracks if struck or over-tightened and can’t be welded like steel. Broken pieces are usually recast from an original.

Mild steel is what almost every new iron-style gate is made from today. It’s strong, can be shaped hot or cold, welds cleanly and costs much less than hand-wrought work. It rusts readily, so its life depends on galvanising.

Many older London gates mix all three: a wrought iron frame with cast iron finials and later steel repairs.

Hand-forged or off-the-shelf?

There’s a big difference between a gate assembled from mass-produced parts and one made by a blacksmith. Budget gates use pressed or cast scrolls and finials welded onto a steel frame. That’s fine from a distance, but the details look thin and identical up close. Hand-forged work has scrolls with tapered, rolled ends, proper collars wrapped around joints instead of blobs of weld, and finials in proportion to the bars. On a listed building or a prominent period frontage, the difference is obvious. We offer both, so the gate can match the house and the budget.

Design details

Traditional gates are built from a familiar set of elements. Bars can be round, square or twisted. Tops can be straight, arched (convex), dipped (concave) or finished with an overthrow, an ornamental arch above a pedestrian gate. Finials come in spears, fleur-de-lis, acorns, pineapples or balls. Scrolls in C and S shapes, collars and rosettes fill the panels. Dog bars are a row of short, closely spaced bars along the bottom that stop small animals slipping through.

The best results come from matching the house and the street. If your neighbours have original railings, a new gate with the same bar spacing, finial pattern and height looks as though it has always been there. Bring us photos of the existing railings, the pillars and nearby properties, and we’ll draw the gate in context before anything is made. A matching pedestrian gate and railings complete the frontage.

Conservation areas and listed buildings

Many London railings were cut down for scrap in the 1940s, and councils are now keen to see them reinstated in the right style. In conservation areas, a new gate generally needs to follow the traditional pattern. Several boroughs, including RBKC and Westminster, publish guidance on appropriate railing and gate designs. For a listed building, altering or replacing historic ironwork usually needs listed building consent, even for what seems like like-for-like work, and carrying out unauthorised works to a listed building is a criminal offence. Gates over 1 metre high next to a road or footpath need planning permission anywhere. Check our borough planning guides before you commit to a design.

Restoring original ironwork

Restoration usually starts with taking the gates off and bringing them to the workshop. There they’re blast-cleaned back to bare metal, so the true condition is visible. Wrought iron is repaired with matching material and traditional methods. Cracked cast iron is repaired by specialist techniques or replaced with new castings made from an original piece. Missing finials and ornaments are recast. Hinges, pivots and latches are rebuilt or renewed.

The finish then depends on the metal. Steel and most wrought iron can be hot-dip galvanised. Cast iron is usually given a zinc-rich primer instead, because the heat of galvanising can crack it. It’s then painted with a traditional system, typically finished in gloss or semi-gloss black. Our restoration article covers the process in more detail. If your gate has a specific fault, such as a dropped leaf or a broken hinge, start with a repair assessment.

Finishes for new gates

New steel gates should be hot-dip galvanised after fabrication, so the zinc coats every weld and the inside of every hollow section. On top of that, a powder coat gives a durable satin finish. For a more historic look, use wet-applied paint in the deep gloss black traditional to London ironwork. Black is the standard, though dark greens and blues appear on some Georgian and Victorian streets and are worth matching if your neighbours have them. See the metal driveway gates page for more on how the finishes compare.

Automating traditional gates

Ornamental steel gates are heavy, often well over 100 kg per leaf, so automation is best planned before the gate is made. Motor brackets are built into the frame and galvanised with it, and the design can be adapted to suit the motor. Underground motors are popular on period frontages because nothing shows above the ground. Ram or articulated arm motors are less expensive and can be mounted discreetly on the inside face. Original gates can sometimes be automated after restoration, but they often need strengthening first and the hinges replaced with heavy-duty pivots. See electric swing gates.

Looking after ironwork

Galvanised and coated new gates need little more than a wash once or twice a year and prompt touching up of any chips. Painted historic ironwork needs more attention. Check for chips, rust bloom and flaking paint each spring, especially on bottom rails and around finials, and plan on repainting every five to eight years. Catching rust early is far cheaper than a full restoration later. Grease the hinges annually and keep drainage holes clear.

Cost of wrought iron gates in London

As a rough guide, a pair of new ornamental steel driveway gates, galvanised and powder-coated, typically costs £3,000 to £7,000 supplied and fitted. Hand-forged bespoke gates usually run from £7,000 to £15,000 or more. Restoring an existing pair is often £1,500 to £5,000, depending on condition and how much recasting is needed. Automation typically adds £2,500 to £6,000. Pier repairs and matching railings are quoted separately. Use our installed cost checklist to compare quotes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are new wrought iron gates actually made of wrought iron?+
Almost never. New iron-style gates are mild steel, often with cast details. True wrought iron is only available as reclaimed material, and it’s mostly used in restoring historic work.
How can I tell if my old gate is wrought iron or cast iron?+
Wrought iron has a fibrous, grainy texture where it’s corroded and often flakes in layers. Its joints are riveted or hand-welded. Cast iron has crisp, moulded ornament, often with faint casting lines, and breaks cleanly rather than bending. We can identify it at survey.
Is it worth restoring my original gates?+
Usually, if they’re genuine wrought or cast iron and the frame is mostly sound. On a listed building, it may be expected. If the gate is later mild steel that’s badly corroded, replacement often makes more sense.
Do I need permission to replace iron gates?+
On a listed building, almost certainly. In a conservation area, possibly, depending on the design and the council. Anywhere, if the gate is over 1 metre high next to a road. Check before ordering.
Does a protective coating mean no maintenance?+
No. A galvanised and coated gate needs very little upkeep, but it should still be washed and touched up when chipped. Traditionally painted ironwork needs repainting every few years.

Driveway & Home Security | A London Guide

Start with the way you use your entrance, then choose improvements that address its weak points. This guide brings together vehicle security, gates and locks, cameras, lighting and access arrangements for London homes.

Short takeaway

Secure the car, the house and the boundary together. Keep gates and locks working, protect keys, and agree how residents and visitors get in. Cameras and lighting support those measures. Choose gates or bollards around the actual driveway, and keep pedestrian access and powered-gate safety in the design. No single product guarantees protection from theft.
